Microsoft wants to keep more of its AI billions from Nvidia

Microsoft (MSFT) is facing a costly artificial intelligence issue. Two-thirds of the $41 billion in capital expenditures in the latest quarter went to shorter-lived assets such as central processing units and graphics processing units. These are the costly devices that lie behind solutions like Copilot and Azure. Microsoft now wants to retain a larger portion of that expenditure inside the company. With multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, Microsoft will use its Maia chips to run AI inference across its products and services. There is an obvious potential loser if Microsoft succeeds: Nvidia (NVDA). One of the large cloud firms purchasing Nvidia chips to develop AI infrastructure is Microsoft. Microsoft may not need to run all of its workloads on someone else's processors in order to transfer them cheaply onto Maia. There is just one issue. Microsoft's proprietary processors are still "nowhere close" to the more advanced technology of Nvidia or Alphabet (GOOGL), according to Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Mandeep Singh. This creates a test worth billions of dollars. Nvidia doesn't have to be replaced everywhere by Microsoft. Maia only has to become proficient at the AI tasks that Microsoft does millions of times every day. Long after a model has been trained, artificial intelligence may be costly. Computers must provide the answer each time someone asks Copilot a query, requests code from GitHub Copilot, or ultimately dispatches an AI agent to do a job. That process is called inference. Because Microsoft runs such services on a massive scale, even modest efficiency improvements may have a significant impact when replicated over millions of users. Microsoft said its current Maia 200 chip is already serving Copilot workloads. Maia 300, expected to enter production deployments in 2027, is designed to become the company's primary inference system. Microsoft also said the Maia 300 can produce seven times the output of the Maia 200 at full rack size and 40% more AI per megawatt than top GPUs. In other words, the company believes it can get more AI work from the infrastructure and power it currently pays for. Because of the massive expenditure, that is important. Microsoft added nearly $116 billion of property and equipment during fiscal 2026, compared with about $65 billion a year earlier. In the June quarter alone, capital expenditures reached $41 billion. It is not necessary for Microsoft to create a semiconductor that is superior than Nvidia for every use if Maia enables the company to offer Copilot and other repetitive AI tasks at a lower cost.

Boehringer and Microsoft collaborate to explore AI in clinical research

No summary available

Boehringer Ingelheim and Microsoft have entered a strategic collaboration to examine the use of AI in clinical research, beginning with studies in lung health. The partnership focuses on evaluating digital patient twins, which are computer-based models of individual patients constructed from clinic...

Boehringer Ingelheim and Microsoft have entered a strategic collaboration to examine the use of AI in clinical research, beginning with studies in lung health. The partnership focuses on evaluating digital patient twins, which are computer-based models of individual patients constructed from clinical and related data. The companies intend to examine whether these models can forecast disease progression and anticipate patient outcomes under varying circumstances. Initial work will assess the technical and scientific feasibility of the concept across several therapeutic areas through prototyping, modelling, and generating evidence. Researchers will study advanced trial simulation, disease-progression and predictive outcome modelling. The work includes testing whether computational models can support synthetic or hybrid control arms as alternatives to standard clinical control groups. Synthetic arms rely entirely on existing datasets, whereas hybrid arms combine historical data with conventional control subjects. According to the companies, the approach could cut the volume of participants assigned to control cohorts, streamline trial design, and hasten evidence gathering. If successful, the methods may enhance drug development efficiency and allow more trial subjects to receive experimental treatments. Microsoft Germany and Austria corporate vice-president and CEO Agnes Heftberger said: "The collaboration with Boehringer Ingelheim brings together pharmaceutical and scientific expertise with Microsoft's capabilities in AI and engineering. "Germany is home to world-class pharmaceutical research and development. Together, we want to explore how technology could open new opportunities for clinical research." Beyond clinical modelling, the alliance covers data centre modernisation and technical security. Both organisations are examining further joint development initiatives across animal health, commercial processes, and technology infrastructure. The initiative links with Boehringer Ingelheim's broader internal adoption of Microsoft Copilot, accompanied by workforce training, governance measures, and technical infrastructure updates across its human pharmaceutical and animal health operations. Last month, Boehringer Ingelheim and Envisagenics entered a research collaboration and option agreement that aims to validate tumour-specific targets for the development of precision therapies in solid tumours. "Boehringer and Microsoft collaborate to explore AI in clinical research" was originally created and published by Pharmaceutical Technology, a GlobalData owned brand.

A study published on Thursday in 'Science' says it was more than twice as accurate as general physicians at solving complex medical cases. The tool uses an "orchestrator," which acts like a simulated panel of clinical experts working together. First, it decides what to ask about the patient's history. Then it picks which tests to order and reviews the results. It also keeps updating its working hypotheses along the way. Most existing medical AI looks at all the symptoms, labs, and images at once, while Microsoft's tool works through the case in stages instead. The model was tested on more than 300 highly unusual and confusing cases, and the physicians it beat were allowed to use textbooks and the internet. It also did better than human doctors on scenarios drawn from a major database of emergency room admissions. The researchers also found that work-ups designed by the orchestrator cost less than those designed by human doctors. Dr. Dominic King, who leads the health unit at Microsoft AI, said older tests rely on multiple-choice questions. "No patient ever came to see me with a nice summary," he said. Next, Microsoft will work with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston. The team plans to test the tool on triaging patients in emergency department waiting rooms. Could You Have Seen The Run In Microsoft Stock Coming?

This rally followed a period where the shares had lost 17.7% over the six months before July 24. By the end of this r...

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Microsoft (MSFT) stock returned 36.8% from July 24 to October 22, 2026, against 3.7% for the S&P 500. This rally followed a period where the shares had lost 17.7% over the six months before July 24. By the end of this run, investors were paying a much higher price for the same twelve months of Microsoft's earnings. What had Microsoft told investors before July 24? What Microsoft Told Investors Before July 24 Well over a year before the run, management told investors that customers were buying more. On its January 29, 2025 call, management said large companies were beginning to move from small trials to "enterprise-wide deployments", and that commercial bookings, the contracts customers sign for future sales, had increased 67%, a jump the finance chief said was driven by Azure commitments from OpenAI. Six months later, on the July 30, 2025 call, management said Azure, its cloud platform, had passed $75 billion in annual revenue, up 34%. This expansion was more than twice the 14.9% growth Microsoft reported as a whole for fiscal 2025. Company filings reinforced these statements. Microsoft's revenue growth from a year earlier rose from 13.3% in the quarter ended March 2025 to 18.1% in the quarter ended June 2025. Growth was still 18.3% in the quarter ended March 2026, which Microsoft filed on April 29, 2026, before the run. The evidence was public and held steady, but the shares still lost 17.7% in the six months before July 24. How Much More Investors Now Pay For Microsoft's Earnings At the October 22 close, investors paid 28.9 times Microsoft's earnings for the twelve months to June 2026, against 20.7 times at the end of June. The end-of-June multiple was the lowest at any quarter end since fiscal 2017. The business maintained the pace shown in its earlier filings. In the quarter ended June 2026, Microsoft's revenue was $90.0 billion, up 17.7% from a year earlier. The shares rose 15.5% on July 30, 2026, marking the biggest one-day move of the run. Microsoft's performance diverged notably from its mega-cap peers over this three-month span. Alphabet, Amazon and Apple stock each returned 7.9% or less over the same three months. Is Microsoft Still Growing At The Same Pace? On sales, yes. Microsoft's revenue grew between 16.7% and 18.4% from a year earlier in each of the four quarters to June 2026, much the same pace the filings showed before the run. Profit on each dollar of those sales has slipped, however. Microsoft's operating margin fell in each of the last three quarters, dropping from 48.9% in the quarter ended September 2025 to 45.1% in the quarter ended June 2026. This figure remained above the 44.9% of a year earlier. Over the full twelve months, the margin was still 46.8%, against 18.5% for the S&P 500 taken as one company.

Volkswagen workers may get Microsoft AI instead of a raise

You hired people, trained them, and paid them more as they got better at the job. That bargain has been frayin...

Every company eventually has to decide what it will pay for when it can't pay for everything. For most of the last century, major industrial employers answered that question the same way. You hired people, trained them, and paid them more as they got better at the job. That bargain has been fraying for years at Volkswagen, the German group behind VW, Audi, Porsche, Skoda, and Cupra. Its chief executive has spent much of 2026 talking about job cuts, idle factory capacity, and a cost gap with rivals that he puts at roughly 20 percent. If you've ever sat through a budget meeting, you know how this goes. Spending that looks like a cost gets cut. Spending that looks like an investment gets defended, even when money is tight. So when the company finds money for something new, it's worth asking where that money is going and who pays for it. This week, I got an answer. Volkswagen Group (VLKAF) has equipped more than 330,000 employees with Microsoft (MSFT) Copilot, the artificial intelligence assistant built into Word, Excel, Outlook, and Teams, Microsoft said on Oct. 21. The timing is hard to miss. Two days earlier, Volkswagen's own labor representatives said the company wants to hold salaries at 2026 levels for the rest of the decade. The rollout did not happen overnight. Volkswagen first gave staff broad access to Copilot Chat, the free chat version that comes with eligible Microsoft 365 plans, and saw more than 300,000 monthly active users on it, according to Microsoft's announcement. Employees are now using a more advanced version tied to what Microsoft calls Work IQ. The company says it reaches into engineering, production, procurement, and sales. "The real value of AI comes from making it available at scale in everyday work," said Sophie Vassarotti, head of group data and AI at Volkswagen Group, in the same release. Related: Franklin Templeton CEO says AI is hiding a bigger tech story Microsoft framed the deal as a template for other industrial companies. "Volkswagen shows how companies can evolve AI from a personal productivity tool into a foundation for future AI innovation," said Agnes Heftberger, chair of the management board of Microsoft Germany. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella cheered the news himself. "Super to see Volkswagen Group putting Copilot to work across the company!" he wrote in an X post on Oct. 22. Here's what the deal looks like by the numbers: More than 330,000 employees are equipped with Copilot, and more than 26,000 AI agents are active across the group over the past month, according to Microsoft About 660,000 people are on Volkswagen's payroll worldwide, including 275,000 in Germany, according to Daily Sabah, which carried the wire report $30 per user per month, paid yearly, for Microsoft 365 Copilot for enterprise, according to Microsoft's pricing page More than 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats across all customers as of July, according to Nadella on Microsoft's fiscal fourth-quarter call, as reported by UC Today

How much MSFT stock does Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella actually own?

No summary available

Not many people remember this, but when Satya Nadella took the reins as CEO of Microsoft in February 2014, the company was struggling to find its place amidst a tech landscape dominated by Apple's smartphones, Google's Android operating system, and Amazon's cloud computing services. Under the leade...

Not many people remember this, but when Satya Nadella took the reins as CEO of Microsoft in February 2014, the company was struggling to find its place amidst a tech landscape dominated by Apple's smartphones, Google's Android operating system, and Amazon's cloud computing services. Under the leadership of Steve Ballmer, Microsoft had undertaken a contentious $7.2 billion acquisition of Nokia's mobile phone business in 2013. That deal ultimately failed, resulting in billions in write-downs and thousands of layoffs. But Nadella did not turn the company around overnight. Over the next few years, he shifted Microsoft's business model even further into cloud computing by expanding Azure and its subscription-based services. He also made strategic acquisitions, including LinkedIn, GitHub, and Minecraft, while investing billions into artificial intelligence before it became a household name. In fact, you could say that Nadella was instrumental in Microsoft's partnership with OpenAI, as he even personally stepped in to serve as mediator when OpenAI's board briefly fired its CEO and co-founder, Sam Altman, in the fall of 2023. Although Microsoft and OpenAI renegotiated their once-exclusive partnership, Microsoft hasn't lost momentum. Their newest agreement, announced in April 2026, gave each greater independence and allowed Microsoft to continue to expand its own AI capabilities through Azure's cloud services. MSFT crossed the trillion-dollar valuation threshold on April 25, 2019, and it hasn't looked back since. In its most recent earnings, the company reported that Azure revenue grew by 43% year-over-year. These results show that Microsoft isn't just one of the founders of the digital era — it's very much a power player, and as the driver behind its innovation, Nadella himself has been rewarded handsomely through salary increases, bonuses, and enormous stock awards. As of Microsoft's latest Proxy statement for fiscal 2025, filed in September 2025, Satya Nadella owned 900,572 shares of Microsoft, equating to about 0.01% of the company's total outstanding shares. Given MSFT's October 19 closing share price of $533.52, those shares would be worth a whopping $480.4 million. But Nadella isn't Microsoft's biggest individual shareholder — not by a long shot. That distinction actually belongs to Steve Ballmer, who is estimated to still own approximately 319 million shares, or roughly 4% of Microsoft. Despite Ballmer stepping down amid Microsoft's struggles, he still owns more than 350 times as much as Nadella's stake.

Top publicly listed companies such as Microsoft (Nasdaq: MSFT), Google parent Alphabet (Nasdaq: GOOGL), Coreweave (Nasdaq: CRWV), Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS), and McDonald's (NYSE: MCD) have joined hands to protest the inclusion of the tokenized version of their stocks on the OKXICE TSV. As per the public notice issued Oct. 19, the number of companies objecting to the plan is 16, demonstrating growing opposition to the tokenization trend. The companies' protest centres on OKXICE issuing the tokenized version of their stocks. In simple words, tokenization is the process of using blockchain technology to turn real‑world assets like stocks, real estate, U.S. Treasury bills, etc. into digital tokens which can be traded fractionally, 24/7. Crypto companies such as Coinbase Global (Nasdaq: COIN), Robinhood Markets (Nasdaq: HOOD), and OKXICE are at the forefront of the tokenization trend. The tokenized stocks are advantageous to traders who want to buy and sell shares 24/7. They also offer exposure to those from outside the U.S. who don't have access to avenues like the Nasdaq and the NYSE. But they don't offer shareholder rights such as ownership and voting like original stocks do. JPMorgan's answer to the stablecoin threat is here Major gold holder backs NVIDIA challenger BlackRock's iconic fund posts strongest day in over 12 months OKXICE TSV is a proposed tokenized stock trading platform created by OKXICE, a 50-50 joint venture between the NYSE parent Intercontinental Exchange and crypto exchange OKX. The avenue will operate under the innovation exemption published last month by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The exemption lets such platforms offer tokenized versions of the U.S. stocks without registering as exchanges. The latest notice doesn't explain the companies' reasons or if their objection stops TSV from issuing the tokens. However, it says these tokens could be issued by an outside party or the issuer itself, which could give companies a more direct role in the process. ● Maxinsights pays everyday people to wear cameras while they cook, clean, and do their jobs, then turns the footage into training data robots learn from ● MaxLoop, the company's proprietary AI platform, automates quality control of footage as it arrives and cuts the human review team by 90% ● Max...

● Maxinsights pays everyday people to wear cameras while they cook, clean, and do their jobs, then turns the footage into training data robots learn from ● MaxLoop, the company's proprietary AI platform, automates quality control of footage as it arrives and cuts the human review team by 90% ● MaxGlove, a sensor glove, records how hard a hand grips and how heavy an object is, which a camera can't see SANTA CLARA, Calif., October 22, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Maxinsights, the company building the data layer for physical AI, today announced $30 million in seed funding led by PeakXV, with participation from Tola Capital, South Park Commons, INCE Capital, and Alumni Ventures. The company also launched MaxLoop, an agent-in-the-loop system that scores and corrects data collection while it happens, and MaxGlove, a sensor glove for capturing tactile touch and force for a new era of data collection. Investors put $47.4 billion into physical AI in the first half of 2026, nearly four times the total for the second half of 2025. The capital is flowing faster than the data that exists to train it. Robots can only learn to fold a shirt or load a dishwasher by watching people do it thousands of times, and nobody has captured that kind of work at anything close to the scale the models require. The full data stack in one place Competitors stage tasks in mock environments and ask operators to slow their hands so the footage is easier to process. Maxinsights records real work at natural speed in real homes, restaurants, and hotels, so models keep seeing new settings and unplanned moments. Every step from capture to delivery happens in-house Maxinsights operates in five steps: Collect. First-person (egocentric) footage of real people working, captured in the wild by our own global network across varied places, objects, and tasks. Check. Automated and human review of every clip: capture quality, task completion, visibility, sync, metadata. Annotate. Proprietary models label each clip across four layers (environment, task, subtask, instruction) plus hand pose, body motion, and object interactions. Curate. Search and rebalance the corpus by task, scene, geography, behavior, complexity, or whatever a client needs. Deliver. Ship raw or processed datasets, then feed client and model feedback into the next collection cycle. The company has captured more than 2 million hours, with 1.5 million hours model-ready and available for immediate delivery. Maxinsights serves over 30 customers, including frontier AI labs and foundation model companies, with eight on recurring contracts.

Infragistics to Strengthen Blazor Development with Microsoft

No summary available

Infragistics Expands Its Open-Source Commitment with Direct Contributions to Blazor and the Broader .NET Community Enterprise UI for Every Blazor App Cranbury, NJ, Oct. 22, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Infragistics, the global software company behind the UI and UX solutions powering applications for t...

Infragistics Expands Its Open-Source Commitment with Direct Contributions to Blazor and the Broader .NET Community Enterprise UI for Every Blazor App Cranbury, NJ, Oct. 22, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Infragistics, the global software company behind the UI and UX solutions powering applications for the world's largest enterprises and software developers, announced its work with Microsoft to advance Blazor. As the .NET ecosystem and its global developer community continue to grow, Infragistics is bringing its nearly four decades of experience building enterprise-ready UX and UI solutions for Morgan Stanley, Société Générale, Infosys, Canon and more, directly into Blazor's continued evolution. Through the collaboration, Infragistics will add new features, address bugs and contribute directly to Blazor and the broader Microsoft .NET ecosystem. Infragistics' work with Microsoft builds on its growing investment in open-source development and the Blazor community. In late 2025, Infragistics made 50 of its Ignite UI controls open source across Blazor for the first time, anchored by a free, open-source data grid backed by decades of enterprise data grid expertise. The release also includes UI components like Grid Lite, Combo Box, Tile Manager, Tree, Stepper and more. Available without a commercial license, the controls give developers greater flexibility to build, customize and extend modern Blazor applications while contributing to publicly visible code. Those controls sit within the broader Ignite UI for Blazor library, which includes the full set of Data Grids, Dock Manager and charts in addition to the open-source components. Infragistics' open-source commitment is now extending directly into Blazor itself. Infragistics has dedicated engineering resources primarily to .NET 11 development in Blazor, with engineers contributing feature enhancements and bug fixes. Those contributions become part of the framework, extending Infragistics' impact to improve the Blazor experience for the broader Blazor community. Infragistics is also open sourcing its MIT-licensed Blazor wrapper for ApexCharts, one of the world's most widely used JavaScript charting libraries with more than 1.5 million weekly NPM installs. The wrapper gives Blazor developers a native C# API for building 17 chart types, making ApexCharts easier for .NET developers to use within Blazor applications. Infragistics has brought its Blazor products and components through Microsoft's own compliance process for security and accessibility, to meet the same standards Microsoft holds for its own frameworks. Ignite UI will now be surfaced through Visual Studio scaffolder and project templates, bringing Infragistics components more directly into the workflow developers use to start new Blazor applications. With more than 7 million .NET developers using the Visual Studio family of products each month, the integration expands how easily developers can discover and access Ignite UI.

Apple is taking Wall Street's top spot back from Nvidia — for the fifth time

No summary available

Apple (AAPL) is taking Wall Street's crown back from Nvidia — for the fifth time. Apple briefly topped Nvidia in market value on Friday. It's a move Apple has made before, and it has rarely stuck. Apple and Nvidia (NVDA) are each worth about $5.1 trillion, and the gap between them was less than 1%...

Apple (AAPL) is taking Wall Street's crown back from Nvidia — for the fifth time. Apple briefly topped Nvidia in market value on Friday. It's a move Apple has made before, and it has rarely stuck. Apple and Nvidia (NVDA) are each worth about $5.1 trillion, and the gap between them was less than 1% at Thursday's close. The flip came alongside a record run for Apple's stock and the day the tech giant's $1,999 iPhone Duo hit stores, capping a battle investors had been watching all morning. Nvidia has since moved back into the lead. For most of the past decade, this wasn't much of a contest. Apple closed as the most valuable US-listed company in about 7 of every 10 sessions since October 2015. Microsoft (MSFT) took the top spot in stretches, Amazon (AMZN) held it for 12 sessions in early 2019, and Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) got exactly one day in 2016. Then the AI boom rewrote the leaderboard. Nvidia first closed at No. 1 on June 18, 2024. It has held the spot almost without a break since June 2025, interrupted only by a four-session Apple run in late July. Apple has reclaimed the crown from Nvidia four times before today. Only once did it last, when the DeepSeek scare sank chip stocks in January 2025 and Apple held on into the spring. Since the start of 2024, the No. 1 spot has changed hands two dozen times, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. This time, the two stocks are heading in opposite directions. Apple closed Thursday at a record. Nvidia sits about 11% below its Oct. 6 record close after this month's chip rout. Since that Oct. 6 close, which was also the S&P 500's (^IXIC) record, Apple is the only megacap stock in the green. It's up 4%. Watch whether Apple can finish the day on top. It hasn't since July 30. The next big test comes on Wednesday, when Microsoft and Alphabet report earnings. They rank third and fourth, each worth about $3.9 trillion. Preorders for the company's first foldable smartphone sold out almost immediately last week, with delivery times currently pushed out well in...

Apple's (AAPL) iPhone Duo goes on sale today, but limited supplies and long lines outside Apple Stores mean you'll have to be lucky to get your hands on one. Preorders for the company's first foldable smartphone sold out almost immediately last week, with delivery times currently pushed out well into late January. Apple said it planned to have some Duos available in stores but expects them to sell out quickly. "On Friday morning, our teams look forward to welcoming customers at Apple Stores to experience iPhone Duo and the incredible iPhone line-up for themselves," Apple said in a statement earlier this week. "Apple Stores will have limited iPhone Duo available for walk-in customers, and we're working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible." At least some of the preorder madness comes down to scalpers hawking the foldable iPhone on sites like eBay at a stiff markup. While the iPhone Duo starts at $1,999, sellers are asking for upwards of $4,000 for the base model. At least one seller is offering a Duo with 2TB of storage, which Apple sells for $3,199, for a staggering $15,000. The Duo is one of Apple's most anticipated products in years. The biggest update to the company's most important device since it launched in 2007, the iPhone Duo could help raise the iPhone's average selling price, boosting Apple's bottom line. The iPhone represented $209.58 billion of Apple's $416.16 billion in total revenue in 2025. That's well ahead of the company's second-largest business segment, Services, which brought in $109.15 billion. The Duo also comes as Apple revamps its iPhone release schedule. Rather than debuting its full lineup of phones at its annual September event last month, Apple revealed only its top-tier smartphones, including the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. The company is widely expected to unveil its standard iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 early next year. The smartphone maker limited pre-orders to two devices per customer, while walk-in availability varied by market. Its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, starts at $1,999 for 256GB and runs to $3,199 for 2TB, according to Channel Insider. That puts the entry model $700 above the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Apple's new CEO pitched it big. The Duo is "the most transformational change to iPhone since the original," John Ternus said at the Sept. 9 launch event, CFJC Today reported. Buyers lined up despite the price tag. The Duo sold out within minutes of preorders opening on Oct. 16, and new orders now ship in January, Dexerto reported. Some confirmed preorders resold on eBay for close to $5,000. Now, one of YouTube's most-watched tech reviewers is telling most of those shoppers to hold on to their cash. Marques Brownlee posted his full iPhone Duo review on Oct. 21, two days before the phone is due to reach stores on Oct. 23. Brownlee spent about a week and a half with the Duo before publishing. His short version is that Apple's first foldable is "polished around the edges, but kind of rough in the middle," according to Dexerto. For people who already own an iPhone and are wondering whether to trade up, his answer was blunt. For most of them, it's probably no. Related: AT&T CEO drops 4-word verdict on new Apple iPhone Duo He also named the buyers who should walk away. That list includes people who mostly text, scroll social media and browse the web, anyone who picks a phone for its camera, and anyone who tends to break phones, Dexerto reported. That last group matters more than it sounds, as the repair math below shows. The problems Brownlee flagged sit in the features you touch most often, from unlocking the phone to opening your favorite apps. More Apple News: Apple's $1,999 foldable iPhone creates strange twist for Samsung Bank of America resets Apple stock price target after iPhone Duo launch Bank of America finds a quicker path to Apple's iPhone Duo Here are the four issues behind his verdict: Apps that don't fit yet: Spotify, Google Maps, Discord, X and Google Calendar aren't properly optimized, showing black bars on the outer screen or shrunken layouts on the inner one. He called app support the Duo's biggest weakness at launch, Dexerto reported. No Face ID: Apple swapped it for a fingerprint reader in the power button, with a built-in delay that makes unlocking feel slow. He expects it to be the feature former iPhone users miss most, according to Dexerto's account of the review. Extra bulk: Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 is noticeably thinner and more than 20% lighter, he said, per Dexerto. Weaker cameras: There's no dedicated zoom lens and no ProRes or Log video, and low-light shots land closer to the budget iPhone 17e than to the Pro models, MacDailyNews reported.

How much Apple stock does CEO John Ternus actually own?

Ternus has worked at Apple for more than two decades, and as CEO, he's likely to be awarded significant amounts of shares based on performance. ...

John Ternus took over as CEO of Apple in September 2026, becoming the iPhone maker's second chief executive since the death of founder Steve Jobs in 2011. Ternus has worked at Apple for more than two decades, and as CEO, he's likely to be awarded significant amounts of shares based on performance. Here's a closer look at how many Apple shares Ternus owns now, early in his tenure as chief executive. John Ternus owned 59,567 shares in Apple, according to an SEC filing on October 5, 2026. His stake represents just a tiny fraction of the company's 14.59 billion shares outstanding. Ternus's shares were valued at over $20.2 million based on a mid-October 2026 share price of $339.50. Related: John Ternus's net worth as Apple's new CEO Compared to other members of Apple's board, Ternus is a relatively minor insider shareholder, at least for now. Arthur D. Levinson owned 3.7 million shares, according to an SEC filing in May 2026; he has been accumulating Apple shares since joining the board of directors in 2000. Tim Cook, whom Ternus replaced as CEO, and who now serves as executive chair of Apple's board, owned 3.2 million shares, according to an October 2026 SEC filing. His shares were primarily derived from stock awards in the form of restricted stock units (RSUs) for meeting the company's internal performance-based goals during his tenure as CEO. Levinson and Cook disclosed their Apple shareholdings as board members under disclosure rules. It is possible (but relatively unlikely) that there are other individuals who own more shares than Cook or Levinson but aren't required to disclose their ownership because their stake doesn't represent 5% or more of the company. (A 5% stake in Apple would be equivalent to nearly 730 million shares.) Institutional investors own the biggest individual stakes in Apple. Institutional ownership in Apple amounted to 76.6% of total shares, according to Nasdaq. The Vanguard Group was the largest institutional investor, with a 9.8% stake. BlackRock (8%) and Vanguard Capital Management (6.6%) rounded out the top three. More on Apple: Apple's stock split history: Everything you need to know Apple's dividend explained: Yield, history & more Where is Apple's headquarters? Apple Park explained Ternus first joined Apple on the company's product design team in 2001, and he eventually worked his way up to senior vice president overseeing hardware engineering, reporting to his predecessor, Cook, before becoming CEO himself. As he was promoted over two decades, he was awarded shares and likely sold some shares along the way.

One of those was Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), which he regretted not buying sooner. However, he remedied that mistake by purchasing shares not long before leaving his role. Current CEO Greg Abel has kept purchasing Alphabet shares, showing that he's also bullish on the stock. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Another stock that Buffett identified as a major value opportunity right away was Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) in the mid-2010s. This turned out to be one of Buffett's best investments ever, and while Berkshire has sold off the number of Apple shares it owns compared to its peak holdings, it's still the largest position in its portfolio. The question is, between the two, which one is the better buy now? I think it's Alphabet, but the answer to that question may depend on whether you're bullish on AI or not. Alphabet and Apple are taking two distinct approaches to the emerging AI landscape. Alphabet is going all-in on AI, and plans to spend about $200 billion on data center capital expenditures this year. The uses for these data centers range from being rented out via its cloud computing unit (a very profitable endeavor) to being used for compute capacity for its Gemini platform (not profitable right now). Regardless, Alphabet has positioned itself as an AI-first investment, but there are those who may be a bit wary regarding Alphabet's all-in position on an emerging technology. Apple is taking the complete opposite approach. Instead of rapidly increasing its AI computing power, it's choosing to deploy Google's Gemini model on its devices, cutting development costs substantially. While it will have to pay to utilize Gemini, the cost to develop a new model may have been far higher in infrastructure and research and development (R&D) expenses. Furthermore, the AI features that Apple has rolled out are lackluster to some, although the revamped Siri AI is receiving positive reviews. Apple still has a long way to go before AI is a top product, and it could lose market share in the smartphone market to some Android phones that are pioneering this technology.

So, strong corporate earnings will be necessary to keep this bull market going. Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) is one of the companies at the center of the AI boom. It operates an industry-leading cloud platform, develops its own large language models (LLMs), and even designs its own data center chips. It's scheduled to release its operating results for the third quarter on Oct. 29, and they will give investors some insight into the current state of the AI industry. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Amazon stock looks attractively valued right now, so is it a buy heading into the report? Amazon Web Services (AWS) is Amazon's cloud computing platform, which offers a growing portfolio of tools and services that enterprises need to develop and deploy AI software. It's consistently the company's fastest growing business segment, and it's also the most profitable, so its results will be Wall Street's main focus on Oct. 29. AWS operates state-of-the-art data centers all over the world which house advanced AI chips from suppliers like Nvidia, and it rents the computing capacity to its enterprise customers. However, Amazon also designs its own chips now, like Trainium2 and Trainium3, which it says offer better price-performance than the competition. Amazon not only rents these chips, but also sells them to customers, and sales revenue was tracking at an annualized rate of over $25 billion on June 30. This could become a huge business over the long term, so look out for some updated numbers on Oct. 29. In addition to computing capacity, enterprises also need ready-made LLMs to sit at the foundation of their AI software projects, and the AWS Bedrock platform offers a library of 100 of them. AWS also built an AI-powered coding assistant called Kiro that can help programmers bring software to life more quickly. AWS generated $42.2 billion in total revenue during the second quarter of 2026, up 37% from the year-ago period. That growth rate accelerated for the fourth-straight period, so the platform was carrying significant momentum into the third quarter.

Yet its free cash flow, the cash left after paying for new buildings and equi...

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Amazon.com (AMZN) earned $135 billion in net income over the four quarters ended June 2026, well above its $93.7 billion of operating income. Yet its free cash flow, the cash left after paying for new buildings and equipment, was a negative $11.6 billion over the same twelve months. That gap is the number a holder should watch, because a company spending more cash than it brings in has to cover the difference somewhere. So where is all that cash going? Amazon Is Spending Its Cash On AI Data Centers Most of it is funding new capacity for AWS, Amazon's cloud business, and for generative AI. During the June quarter alone, Amazon spent $53.1 billion in cash on capital projects, compared with the $45.4 billion in cash its operations brought in. Management said this spending supports strong customer demand. Even at its planned spending for the year, management said Amazon will not have enough capacity to meet all the demand it sees in 2026. Management believes the same will be true in 2027. The bill is also growing. Management now expects about $220 billion of cash capital spending in 2026, up from its earlier estimate of about $200 billion, because memory costs more. How Fast Has Amazon's Free Cash Flow Fallen? Amazon's free cash flow has fallen in each of the last two twelve-month periods. The figure stood at $48.3 billion in the twelve months from July 2023 to June 2024, dropped to $13.5 billion from July 2024 to June 2025, and then turned negative in the latest twelve months. Debt has climbed over the same stretch. Amazon's total debt reached $223 billion at the end of June 2026, up from $134 billion a year earlier. Management also said on its July 30, 2026 call that the company has issued debt in 2026. The wait for a return is long, too. Management said Amazon begins spending data center money two years before it can put servers into the buildings and start earning from them. So some of the money Amazon spends today will not earn anything for a while. What Are Amazon Investors Paying For Now? Investors pay 19.9 times Amazon's earnings, against 23.0 for the S&P 500. That multiple looks low partly because Amazon's net income, lifted by items outside its main operations, sits well above its operating income. Measured against operating income, investors pay about 28.8 times. The best case against the worry is that much of the demand is already signed. Management said Amazon's backlog stood at $496 billion on the July call, growing at a triple-digit rate from a year earlier. AWS revenue grew 36.7% from a year earlier in the June quarter. Management also said servers and networking equipment take a little less than three years to break even, while most of its AI capacity is contracted for at least five-year terms. Because Amazon buys servers only a few months before putting them to use, it will not spend that money if the demand is not there, management added.

Amazon caught hackers probing a PHP flaw 4 days before the fix

No summary available

Most security breaches start with a lock nobody knew was broken. For years, that was the comfortable assumption behind the software that runs the internet. Bugs existed, but finding the dangerous ones took rare skill and a lot of time. That buffer has quietly disappeared. Artificial intelligence i...

Most security breaches start with a lock nobody knew was broken. For years, that was the comfortable assumption behind the software that runs the internet. Bugs existed, but finding the dangerous ones took rare skill and a lot of time. That buffer has quietly disappeared. Artificial intelligence is now finding old flaws faster than humans can patch them, and attackers are using the same tools to turn fixes into weapons. If you have a website for your business, your side hustle or your church, this one lands on you too. The fix is free and already out. The hard part is getting it onto millions of servers before attackers get there first, and that race started earlier than most people realize. It also explains why Wikipedia, the Port of Rotterdam, and France's Interior Ministry all pulled sites offline on Oct. 21. I spent the morning going through the disclosures, and one detail stands out more than any outage list. Amazon (AMZN) says its security team caught someone trying to exploit the newly discovered flaws in PHP, the programming language behind most of the web, on Oct. 17. That was four days before the developers released a fix, according to a post on Amazon's security blog. Read more: IBM, Amazon quantum pricing gets a challenger in Postquant Labs Amazon runs decoy servers, known as honeypots, to watch what attackers do. One of them recorded an exploit attempt from an anonymized internet address while the flaws were still under embargo, wrote CJ Moses, chief information security officer of Amazon Integrated Security. It is still unclear how the attacker learned about the bugs early. Moses said proof-of-concept exploits were circulating as early as 2 a.m. UTC on Oct. 21, about 12 hours before the official release. "PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild," Moses wrote. More Technology: Anthropic announces big plan to help workers disrupted by AI Chip toolmakers can't catch a break, even as TSMC spends more Apple's new CEO just teamed up with Tim Cook's old rival The flaws, tracked as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entries CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, let an attacker run code on a vulnerable server without logging in. Cybersecurity firm Wiz, which Alphabet (GOOGL) owns, said it found them with help from its own AI tool plus Google's Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, according to its research post. Wiz said the bugs reach back to PHP 5.4 and had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. "Applying the PHP security update remains the only complete remediation," the firm wrote.

This is essentially a reflection of how the covering analysts have collectively reassessed their initial estimates over this period. Investors should keep in mind that the direction of estimate revisions by each of the covering analysts may not always get reflected in the aggregate change. Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise Estimate revisions ahead of a company's earnings release offer clues to the business conditions for the period whose results are coming out. This insight is at the core of our proprietary surprise prediction model -- the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction). The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a more recent version of the Zacks Consensus EPS estimate. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier. Thus, a positive or negative Earnings ESP reading theoretically indicates the likely deviation of the actual earnings from the consensus estimate. However, the model's predictive power is significant for positive ESP readings only. A positive Earnings ESP is a strong predictor of an earnings beat, particularly when combined with a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), 2 (Buy) or 3 (Hold). Our research shows that stocks with this combination produce a positive surprise nearly 70% of the time, and a solid Zacks Rank actually increases the predictive power of Earnings ESP.

Previously, he was Managing Director at AlTi Global and spent nearly a decade at the U.S. Treasury Department in senior policy and intelligence roles across Europe, Africa and the Middle East. "Replit empowers every American, and every global citizen, to be the architect of their own future," said Greenwald. Google and Voltus have announced an expanded agreement to build a virtual power plant (VPP) with a total capacity of 1GW in the Pennsylvania-New Jersey-Maryland (PJM) grid region, which covers 13 US states and Washington, DC. The agreement increases the planned capacity nearly tenfold from a prior 100MW deal signed in June 2026. Voltus, which operates a distributed energy resource (DER) platform, will aggregate energy capacity from local businesses and households for the VPP, which will be funded by Google. The VPP aims to strengthen grid reliability during periods of high demand by using a combination of batteries, smart thermostats and industrial flexibility. These resources can be signalled by Voltus to reduce consumption or adjust usage, helping to alleviate stress on the grid. Participants in the scheme are expected to receive economic benefits including potential bill savings and direct payments, linked to their role in providing flexible capacity. According to the companies, the total capacity outlined in the agreement represents one of the largest distributed energy portfolios managed by a hyperscale company in the region to date. Google North and South America energy market development head Ellen Zuckerman said: "Distributed energy resources are powerful tools for managing a modern, reliable grid while keeping energy affordable. "Expanding our initial commitment tenfold demonstrates our core effort to actively bring our own capacity to the grids that serve us. "Procuring this capacity through a gigawatt-scale virtual power plant ensures Google's operations in PJM support regional reliability and deliver direct economic benefits to local communities." The PJM grid region serves around 67 million people. Voltus CEO Dana Guernsey said: "This significant expansion of our work with Google translates data centre growth into direct economic benefits for businesses and homes. Through this partnership we are proud to bring much needed clean capacity online, at gigawatt scale." Last month, MN8 Energy, Eos Energy Enterprises and Google launched a collaborative project in West Virginia, US, with the goal of providing additional clean energy resources to the PJM grid to help meet rising demand in the area. Eric Schmidt spent nearly a decade atop Google as its CEO, steering the tech giant from its early days as a public company to its current status as one of the world's most valuable businesses. But the job wasn't always about launching the next Gmail or Google Maps. Instead, much of Schmidt's time was actually spent at a conference room table coordinating people and putting out fires across the organization. "I used to tell people, 'My job is to sit in meetings 12 hours a day, five days a week, and I work on the weekend, too,'" Schmidt said in conversation with Nicolai Tangen, CEO of Norges Bank Investment Management. "I would sit in meetings 12 hours a day—person, person, person, reason, narrative, so forth, and so on." That extended his workweek to roughly 63 hours, Schmidt estimated. But the 71-year-old now believes AI can increasingly handle tasks that once required hours of meetings and conversations across departments. "Much of that coordination tax can be eliminated by these AI platforms for business," he said. Schmidt pointed to an unnamed friend who recently laid off 20% of his workforce. Among those let go, he said, were the employees responsible for planning, coordinating, and moving information around the business—the "glue people" who helped keep the organization running behind the scenes. Schmidt expects that kind of workforce reduction to become more common as AI makes businesses more efficient. "Let's say you're running a 10,000-person company, my guess is you've got a couple of thousand people who you don't need," Schmidt said. "And you better figure out a way to legally and humanely transition them, retire them out, or what have you. You just don't need them." Schmidt, who has an estimated net worth of $66 billion, is expected to be one of the greater beneficiaries of the AI boom. It was revealed this week that he owns roughly a 1% stake in Anthropic, which could translate into a $20 billion windfall if the AI giant goes public at its $2 trillion target. Despite his prediction that AI could make thousands of existing jobs unnecessary, Schmidt also sees opportunities for workers who can adapt to the technology—and help build what comes next. "You're going to need the great inventors, the great salespeople, because it's a human deal," Schmidt said. "You're going to need some great leaders. And you're going to need people to talk to the government."

Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian added in SiliconANGLE's same-day report: "We are focused on giving customers a broad selection of models, including those from OpenAI, so they can choose the right model for any given job, helping to deliver optimal quality and lower costs." Google Cloud becomes the third hyperscaler to sell OpenAI's models since its exclusive Azure distribution ended in April, after Amazon Bedrock (April 28) and Oracle Cloud (June 10). The distribution went multi-cloud. The watts underneath it did not. The commercial terms are the first thing to read carefully, because they are mostly absent. Neither Google Cloud nor OpenAI published per-token pricing for any of the three models as sold through Model Garden as of the announcement date. Access is a private preview for select enterprise customers, with general availability reported as coming in the weeks ahead and no firm date. Public Model Garden documentation did not list any OpenAI model; model IDs, supported regions, quotas, and rate cards required a signed-in console. This is not an open marketplace listing. It is a negotiated enterprise channel whose terms are not public until you are in the room — the same architecture as the $20 million license gates this beat tracks, applied to distribution instead of licensing. The billing mechanics deserve one precise note. Google's Flexible Savings Plans allow drawdown across model providers, but Google's own FSP documentation states: "Third-party products don't get any discounts from the FSP." Spend on third-party models under an FSP draws down against your organization's enterprise commitment, subject to the standard Cloud Marketplace drawdown rules and contract caps defined in the enterprise agreement. A CIO counting on FSP economics for GPT-6 Astra usage is counting on terms that Google has not published.

Google supersizes PJM virtual power plant to more than 1 GW

This story was originally published on Utility Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily Utility Dive newsletter. Google is expanding its efforts to contract distributed capacity to help meet its power needs in the PJM Interconnection with the addition of 1,070 MW to an ...

This story was originally published on Utility Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily Utility Dive newsletter. Google is expanding its efforts to contract distributed capacity to help meet its power needs in the PJM Interconnection with the addition of 1,070 MW to an initial 100-MW virtual power plant agreement it signed with Voltus in June, the companies said Thursday. Under the agreement, Google will pay Voltus to aggregate distributed resources from residential, commercial and industrial customers. The resources can include batteries, smart thermostats, on-site generation, industrial process adjustments and other flexible assets that can reduce energy use, the companies said. Voltus will offer the combined resources into PJM's market when the grid is strained, they said. Such contracts signal a turning point for distributed resources in energy markets, industry sources say. In previous comments to Utility Dive, Voltus CEO Dana Guernsey compared them to the power purchase agreements that unlocked financing for utility-scale wind and solar. Voltus expects to ramp up to the VPP's full capacity over three to four years and then to run it under a contract with Google through 2040, Sarah Spitz, a spokesperson for the San Francisco-based demand response company, told Utility Dive in an email. PJM, the largest U.S. wholesale power market, oversees the grid in 13 states and the District of Columbia. The grid operator has recently fallen short of its reliability margins despite skyrocketing capacity auction prices, due in large part to rising demand from data centers. Demand response revenue in PJM jumped 240% from 2024 to 2025, reaching $523.5 million, mainly due to higher capacity prices and increases in capacity market revenue, Monitoring Analytics, the grid operator's market monitor, said in its annual market report released in March. Emergency demand response accounted for 88% of all demand response revenue, the market monitor added. Energy users in PJM can earn up to $350,000/MW-year through demand response-related payments, according to Voltus. In addition to providing direct financial benefits for VPP participants, virtual power plants can put downward pressure on electric rates by reducing peak demand, according to a report The Brattle Group released this month. Voltus has about 8.5 GW of distributed assets under contract across North America, according to the company. It aims to have 20 GW under contract by the end of this decade, in part by advancing its Bring Your Own Capacity initiative, the company said earlier this month, after it raised $225 million in its latest funding round.

Meta raised the lower end of its capital expenditure estimates to between $135 billion and $145 billion from $130 billion and $145 billion. The company also has $825 billion in various spending commitments related to cloud capacity arrangements, energy service agreements, and consumer hardware products. Despite Wall Street's reaction to Meta's earnings, analysts were largely bullish on the company's outlook, owing to its prospects for its Muse AI agent and models. CEO Mark Zuckerberg repeatedly pointed to Muse as a source of growth potential during the company's earnings call, saying that "Muse will be highly profitable over multiple years," as long as compute efficiency in AI systems continues to improve. Read more: Meta's Muse says it can manage your money. Should you let it? Meta posted an all-time high revenue of $64 billion in the quarter, well ahead of the $63.3 billion analysts anticipated. GAAP earnings per share came in at $3.83 versus expectations of $3.56, but would have been $7.40 without legal charges related to the company's teen mental health settlement. The company also announced it will issue new nonvoting Class C shares to all Class A stockholders, effectively creating a 2-for-1 stock split. The move is meant to ensure Zuckerberg stays in California and retains voting control of the company if the state's Proposition 40 passes on Election Day. Proposition 40 calls for a 5% tax on taxpayers with assets over $1 billion. Big Tech's capex spending looks different this year as Meta and Tesla save for later

No summary available

When will investors see returns on all that AI spending? That's the nagging question facing tech companies quarter after quarter. The AI build-out sounds nice, but shareholders are craving returns on those investments. The easiest way to improve margins, as any corporate consultant knows, is to wat...

When will investors see returns on all that AI spending? That's the nagging question facing tech companies quarter after quarter. The AI build-out sounds nice, but shareholders are craving returns on those investments. The easiest way to improve margins, as any corporate consultant knows, is to watch spending. And in high-rate environments, spending less and showing financial discipline is rewarded even more. Meta (META), Tesla (TSLA), and SpaceX (SPCX) did that for their near-term outlooks, which undershot expectations. That looks different, and welcome. But it was short-lived: The costs were just moved to a different spot on the timeline. Longer-term, off-balance-sheet spending plans of $825 billion for Meta and a $100 billion chip plant estimate for Tesla upended all the goodwill on Thursday — sending markets into a tizzy. A gauge of Meta's credit risk surged to a new record and its bonds sank, Bloomberg reported, after the company said it would spend about $825 billion in the future on computing power, AI infrastructure, and other commitments. Meanwhile, Elon Musk said the chip plant Tesla is building with SpaceX will need tens of billions of dollars in equipment through early 2028 and likely more than $100 billion over the long term. Scaling robots and robotaxis, reusable rockets, and putting data centers in space are things that these companies do not currently do. So it should come as no surprise that it's going to be expensive. After all, that brief list probably has some of the most expensive-sounding things a person could conceive. The bigger truth of these expenses, however, is that they're not yet on balance sheets and represent hopes for massive growth. In other words, hyper-bullish ambition. Even as these companies showed some pleasingly responsible capex numbers on their latest earnings, Zuckerberg and Musk still need to sell their visions above all else. All this stands in stark contrast to Apple (AAPL) and its tremendous rise this year. The company is sitting on its cash pile and watching its peers pour hundreds of billions of dollars into AI tech, proving the point in reverse. In the absence of meaningful AI profits and plenty of AI volatility, a stable hardware business has become Wall Street's favorite tech hedge. Wall Street is fickle. And there's a fine line, apparently, between tech companies spending too much or too little on their AI dreams. Sometimes, pulling back on AI investment isn't received as more disciplined corporate finance, but as taking your foot off the gas pedal.

Investing.com -- Meta's (NASDAQ:META) recent surprise move to issue a new class of non-voting stock has weighed on sentiment toward the AI giant, as Thursday's 7% sell-off shows despite strong earnings. But one of its motives for the move paints a more concerning picture for the AI-dependent stock market. Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list » In its filing, Meta's special committee highlighted that a motivation for the decision was not only to keep CEO Mark Zuckerberg in California but also "an increasingly challenging environment for raising capital," citing recent large capital raises and anticipated capital raises at Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI "to fund the same AI growth." "The Special Committee considered that, while the Company presently has sufficient capital resources for its current needs, in order to finance its funding needs going forward it would be prudent for the Company to do so before even more companies have absorbed available capital in the market," the filing said. Meta expects to use the new Class C shares for equity offerings from time to time, subject to market conditions, and wants them available as early as the end of 2026. The language is striking because it suggests that even one of the world's most profitable technology companies sees access to capital as something that could become increasingly constrained as the AI arms race intensifies. Meta is hardly a company in immediate financial distress. But its filing makes clear that the scale of investment required to compete in AI is changing its financing calculus. The new shares would give it another way to raise money, compensate employees and finance acquisitions without diluting the voting power of existing shareholders. That flexibility could prove valuable as the company commits ever-larger sums to AI infrastructure. More importantly, however, Meta's reasoning raises a broader question for investors: What happens if the companies racing to dominate AI begin competing not just for computing power, but for the capital needed to finance the race itself? The companies competing to dominate AI are embarking on an extraordinary investment cycle. Building and operating increasingly powerful models requires vast computing infrastructure, including specialized chips, data centers, networking equipment and electricity. Those investments must be financed well before their eventual returns are fully established.

Shopping is the most common activity for Meta Platforms' new Muse personal artificial intelligence agent, with an average purchase size of $200, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Wednesday during a conference call to report quarterly income. About 25% of Muse users task it with shopping, including travel planning, he said. Digital payments processor Stripe handles some payments. In the first week of the Muse agent's release last month, Meta "had to work with Stripe to raise credit limits, since the volumes were above what any of us expected," Zuckerberg said, without offering any specifics about agentic transactions or payments. About 10 million people have signed up for a Muse agent, in the U.S. and Canada, the initial two markets, he said. Meta uses Stripe's Link digital wallet as the Muse payment method. Beyond agentic shopping, users' directions to increase their "personal productivity" and connecting Muse to email and calendars are the next most widely used tasks for the service, Zuckerberg said. Meta's third-quarter earnings report Wednesday was its first since the Sept. 8 debut of the personal AI agent. Meta describes the digital agent as one that requires no technical experience and "no learning curve." Stripe charted a significant increase in agentic commerce, starting last month, the company's president, John Collison, said last week, during a podcast he hosts. He described the increase in the bot-driven commerce as he conversed with Zuckerberg, saying the Stripe agentic activity "started going vertical," in September. Collison's brother Patrick Collison, who is Stripe's CEO, sits on Meta's board of directors. Muse, along with personal agents like Instinct, and the open source agent OpenClaw, are viewed by some in the payments industry as the likeliest gateways for agentic commerce to expand into agent-driven consumer transactions. The topic of AI-driven commerce – including agentic transactions and whether a "human in the loop" model will ever yield to fully machine-driven payments – was a major topic of discussion at the annual Money20/20 financial technology conference this week in Las Vegas. Agentic spending remains far from ready for mass public use, with multiple parties in the retail ecosystem still needing to sort out a variety of issues, including liability, Early Warning Services CEO Cameron Fowler said Monday in an interview.

A New Mexico judge just issued a remarkable warning for users of Muse, the new AI-powered bot marketed by Meta Platforms: Sign up for this thing at your own risk. Judge Francis J. Mathew didn't specifically mention Muse in the blistering findings of facts he issued Wednesday, in which he socked Meta with a $25-billion penalty for its "lies" and "false promises" to protect the privacy of its users and keep their personal data secure. Mathew laid out the "systematic pattern of deception" about those issues and others that Meta engaged in over more than a decade. Some of those "lies," as it happens, are very much like the promises Meta has made about the security of Muse. Penalties, consent agreements and decrees have not deterred Meta from using deceptive trade practices. New Mexico Judge Francis J. Mathew As recently as Wednesday, during a conference call for investment analysts about the company's third-quarter financial results, Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg boasted of the "state-of-the art privacy and security" that Meta has vested in Muse. The truth is that throughout its history, as I noted recently and Mathew set forth in great detail, Meta has been a serial violator of its users' privacy. In the past, that has cost the company dearly, though perhaps not enough. In 2019, the Federal Trade Commission hit the company, then known as Facebook, with a record $5-billion fine for violating the terms of a 2011 FTC settlement over privacy practices. I pointed out then that, as big as the fine appeared to be, the company collected that much in revenue in an average month and more than four times as much in profit in a single year. Whether the fine prompted the company to change its ways is hard to gauge. The New Mexico jury that on Sept. 25 found Meta guilty of years of deceit pinpointed numerous allegedly deceptive statements that Zuckerberg, his then-deputy, Sheryl Sandberg, and other executives made after the 2019 fine. But those statements generally involved the company's supposed efforts to cleanse its platform of hate speech, misinformation and incitements to violence rather than claims about privacy protections. Still, the burden of the jury verdict and Judge Mathew's order is that Meta can't be trusted to live up to its promises. Meta's chief legal officer, C.J. Mahoney, told me by email that the judge's ruling, along with the state attorney general's "approach to enforcement ... makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico." Mahoney said the ruling "seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," and that the company will appeal.

Mark Zuckerberg owns 13% of Meta but controls 61% of its votes. California’s wealth tax would bill him on the 13%

No summary available

California voters will decide on Nov. 3 whether the state's billionaires should pay a one-time 5% tax on their net worth. Some of them have already left, like Peter Thiel and Google cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin. They join seven billionaires so far who have publicly moved out of the state, t...

California voters will decide on Nov. 3 whether the state's billionaires should pay a one-time 5% tax on their net worth. Some of them have already left, like Peter Thiel and Google cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin. They join seven billionaires so far who have publicly moved out of the state, taking about $540 billion, or 30% of the state's billionaire wealth. Meanwhile, others like Jensen Huang are staying. Meta's Mark Zuckerberg looked, up until now, as if he would also join Huang in staying in the state where his company is headquartered. But Meta's new SEC filing that posted this week shows that's in part because of the key difference between owning a company and controlling it. Ownership is a share of a company's value. Control is a share of its votes. For most shareholders they are the same because each share carries one vote. At Meta, they are not. Zuckerberg holds mostly Class B shares, which carry 10 votes each. Ordinary Class A shares carry one. So of every $100 of Meta's value, about $13 is his, but of every 100 votes, about 61 are his, according to a filing Meta released Wednesday. That majority lets him elect the entire board and decide nearly every shareholder vote. A wealth tax bills the first number—and to pay it, Zuckerberg would have to sell stock, thereby losing control. When Class B shares are sold, they turn into one-vote Class A shares, so every sale to pay the tax would cut into his control. According to the filing, Meta's board feared that loss of control. According to the committee of independent directors that negotiated with Zuckerberg, they found he was "not on the verge of losing voting control." But it named the wealth tax as one of the main reasons that could change, saying it "has the most significant impact because it would require him to sell shares, or at least borrow against them." The filing says he "could become liable for a significant, multi-billion dollar tax payment based on his ownership of stock in the Company." Zuckerberg also argued that ownership and control don't need to line up. At an Aug. 26 meeting, he "questioned why the preservation of the status quo with respect to the ratio of his voting control to his economic interest in the Company should be a consideration for the Special Committee, citing precedent in other companies where relatively small economic ownership nevertheless conveyed founder voting control," the filing read. That's why the committee proposed in August a dividend of new non-voting stock that would be payable "if, and only if, California Proposition 40 became law and a tax payment by Mr. Zuckerberg became due and payable," sized to cover his bill. Zuckerberg wanted more, saying "he did not wish to go through additional protracted negotiation processes in the future if taxes similar to California Proposition 40 were proposed in other jurisdictions."

Elon Musk's influence over first Tesla (TSLA) and now SpaceX (SPCX) has long been measured in terms of corporate valuations, technological breakthroughs, and personal wealth, where his companies have made him the richest person in the world. Across the last few years, however, the centi-billionaire's growing portfolio of businesses has pushed him into a new lane entirely. Over the past decade, Elon Musk has become far more than a corporate executive or political power broker. Through his control of companies underpinning global communications, military operations, space access, and artificial intelligence, Musk has acquired a degree of influence over national security, international relations, and the global economy that few private individuals have ever possessed. "There's a very real chance that [Musk] is the most powerful civilian, non-governmental actor in history," Gautam Mukunda, a research fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School and managing director of the consultancy Two Rivers Group, told Yahoo Finance. Musk "has resources that are vastly larger than those of all but a handful of governments on the planet." That influence came into sharp focus this month when widely reported restrictions on SpaceX's satellite communications services disrupted Ukraine's military operations, exposing just how dependent a sovereign nation's battlefield capabilities had become on infrastructure supplied by a private-sector company. There are conflicting accounts of who ordered the restrictions in Ukraine, which disrupted battlefield drones and prompted several hours of faltering drone speeds and faulty communications on the front lines of the nation's conflict with Russia. Musk says the White House controls Ukraine's access to Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink funded by the Pentagon, while officials in the Trump administration have said they weren't involved in the decision. Regardless of responsibility, the incident has highlighted the increasing separation between corporate access to governments and governmental reliance on the private sector, particularly given Musk's singular control over rocketry and satellite communications. SpaceX is now responsible for roughly 90% of all mass sent into orbit off Earth, Musk said on SpaceX's recent earnings call. The Pentagon is Starshield's largest customer, while countries such as the Philippines, Argentina, and Indonesia use Starlink for national communications, including emergency services. "He can turn a country's communications on or off — that's an extraordinary power," Darrell West, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution's Center for Technology Innovation, told Yahoo Finance. "Even governments can't do that."

The AI build-out sounds nice, but shareholders are craving returns on those investments. The easiest way to improve margins, as any corporate consultant knows, is to watch spending. And in high-rate environments, spending less and showing financial discipline is rewarded even more. Meta (META), Tesla (TSLA), and SpaceX (SPCX) did that for their near-term outlooks, which undershot expectations. That looks different, and welcome. But it was short-lived: The costs were just moved to a different spot on the timeline. Longer-term, off-balance-sheet spending plans of $825 billion for Meta and a $100 billion chip plant estimate for Tesla upended all the goodwill on Thursday — sending markets into a tizzy. A gauge of Meta's credit risk surged to a new record and its bonds sank, Bloomberg reported, after the company said it would spend about $825 billion in the future on computing power, AI infrastructure, and other commitments. Meanwhile, Elon Musk said the chip plant Tesla is building with SpaceX will need tens of billions of dollars in equipment through early 2028 and likely more than $100 billion over the long term. Scaling robots and robotaxis, reusable rockets, and putting data centers in space are things that these companies do not currently do. So it should come as no surprise that it's going to be expensive. After all, that brief list probably has some of the most expensive-sounding things a person could conceive. The bigger truth of these expenses, however, is that they're not yet on balance sheets and represent hopes for massive growth. In other words, hyper-bullish ambition. Even as these companies showed some pleasingly responsible capex numbers on their latest earnings, Zuckerberg and Musk still need to sell their visions above all else. All this stands in stark contrast to Apple (AAPL) and its tremendous rise this year. The company is sitting on its cash pile and watching its peers pour hundreds of billions of dollars into AI tech, proving the point in reverse. In the absence of meaningful AI profits and plenty of AI volatility, a stable hardware business has become Wall Street's favorite tech hedge. Wall Street is fickle. And there's a fine line, apparently, between tech companies spending too much or too little on their AI dreams. Sometimes, pulling back on AI investment isn't received as more disciplined corporate finance, but as taking your foot off the gas pedal.

Energea Portfolio 4 USA LP ("the Portfolio") has committed up to $20 million to finance the buildout of EV charging stations. The Portfolio's first transaction is a $10 million credit facility to ChargedEV, a developer and owner of Tesla V4 Supercharger stations. The initial draw off the facility is secured by two operating charging stations in Georgia. The capital is intended to fund the expansion of ChargedEV's portfolio in the Southeast United States. Energea is negotiating a similar structure with a second charging station developer. "We see significant opportunities to grow our U.S. portfolio by expanding its scope to broader energy infrastructure investments," said Mike Silvestrini, Co-Founder and Managing Partner at Energea. "The Southeast U.S. continues to experience strong population growth, and to accommodate that growth, more capital is required to fund infrastructure like EV charging stations. We see a growing demand for EV chargers resulting in a new asset class with recurring, energy-based revenue. Having our first investments on the world's most recognized EV charging platform provides a perfect onramp." The financing structure features monthly payments, a fixed interest rate, seven-year amortization of each draw following a short interest-only period, a first-priority secured interest in the charging station assets and an option for the Portfolio to acquire a minority equity interest in the assets at a future date. Energea intends to seek similar investments with more charging station development companies in the U.S. "Investors are seeking differentiated sources of income in their portfolios beyond traditional bonds and corporate lending strategies. Investments secured by operating energy infrastructure are a natural extension of what we've done since inception," said Chris Sattler, Co-Founder and Managing Partner at Energea.
