Media reports about these brokerage-firm-employed (or sell-side) analysts changing their ratings often affect a stock's price. Do they really matter, though? Before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage, let's see what these Wall Street heavyweights think about Nvidia (NVDA). Nvidia currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.13, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 53 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.13 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy. Of the 53 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 49 are Strong Buy and three are Buy. Strong Buy and Buy respectively account for 92.5% and 5.7% of all recommendations. Check price target & stock forecast for Nvidia here>>> While the ABR calls for buying Nvidia, it may not be wise to make an investment decision solely based on this information. Several studies have shown limited to no success of brokerage recommendations in guiding investors to pick stocks with the best price increase potential. Are you wondering why? The vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover often results in a strong positive bias of their analysts in rating it. Our research shows that for every "Strong Sell" recommendation, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations. In other words, their interests aren't always aligned with retail investors, rarely indicating where the price of a stock could actually be heading. Therefore, the best use of this information could be validating your own research or an indicator that has proven to be highly successful in predicting a stock's price movement. Zacks Rank, our proprietary stock rating tool with an impressive externally audited track record, categorizes stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), and is an effective indicator of a stock's price performance in the near future. Therefore, using the ABR to validate the Zacks Rank could be an efficient way of making a profitable investment decision. In spite of the fact that Zacks Rank and ABR both appear on a scale from 1 to 5, they are two completely different measures. The ABR is calculated solely based on brokerage recommendations and is typically displayed with decimals (example: 1.28). In contrast, the Zacks Rank is a quantitative model allowing investors to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5.

In an exclusive statement to Benzinga, Shay Boloor, c...

U.S. restrictions on high-bandwidth memory and semiconductor manufacturing equipment are limiting China's ability to produce advanced AI chips, but experts warn the measures could also accelerate Beijing's efforts to replace American technology. In an exclusive statement to Benzinga, Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Equities, said the restrictions are having a dual effect, constraining Chinese chipmakers in the near term while encouraging domestic suppliers to develop alternatives. "Every restriction also gives Chinese suppliers a larger captive market and stronger incentive to replace foreign technology," Boloor said. Christopher Tang, a professor at the UCLA Anderson School of Management who studies global supply chains, told Benzinga that HBM is the most immediate constraint on China's AI chip production. China accumulated an estimated 13 million HBM stacks before U.S. controls took effect in December 2024, but those reserves are being depleted. Domestic memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) is projected to produce about 2 million stacks in 2026, enough to support an estimated 250,000 to 300,000 Huawei Technologies Ascend-class chips, Tang said. Without access to ASML Holding NV's (NASDAQ:ASML) advanced extreme ultraviolet lithography equipment, Chinese manufacturers rely on older deep ultraviolet technology and multiple patterning techniques, which raise costs and reduce yields. Tang said China could develop chips capable of meeting much of its domestic AI demand within a few years, though matching global leaders at scale could take until late this decade or beyond. Read Also:Vertiv, Nvidia Target 30% More AI Token Output The longer-term consequences could extend beyond China's AI ambitions to American semiconductor companies. Nvidia Corp's (NASDAQ:NVDA) share of China's AI accelerator market has effectively fallen to zero, Tang said. He also noted that Applied Materials Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT) China revenue contribution declined to 28% from 35% a year earlier. Beijing is further encouraging domestic substitution by requiring chipmakers to use at least 50% Chinese-made equipment when expanding capacity, Tang said. While the global AI boom is currently helping offset some lost business, he warned that Chinese equipment suppliers could eventually become stronger international competitors. "The long-term risk for the U.S. is that Chinese suppliers mature in a protected home market and then compete abroad," Tang said.

Taiwan Semiconductor and ASML Are Incredible, but 1 of These Monopoly Chip Stocks Is Far Safer.

No summary available

There are few companies on the market more impressive than Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM) and ASML Holding (NASDAQ: ASML). Both are essentially monopolies for different reasons, but each is an incredible business and has rewarded shareholders with strong stock performance. However, ...

There are few companies on the market more impressive than Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM) and ASML Holding (NASDAQ: ASML). Both are essentially monopolies for different reasons, but each is an incredible business and has rewarded shareholders with strong stock performance. However, these two aren't the same from an investment standpoint. One is far safer, and it all boils down to how much success is priced into the stock. I think Taiwan Semiconductor is the far safer bet for multiple reasons, making it the better investment right now. Here's why. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » There are different types of monopolies, and not all of them are viewed the same way. When it comes to monopolies, ASML is about as good as it gets. It is the only company in the world with the technology to make extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. These machines are about as big as a school bus and cost hundreds of millions of dollars. EUV machines are used by chip fabricators, such as Taiwan Semiconductor, to lay down tiny electrical traces on chips. These traces are microscopic and have spacing as little as 2 nanometers (nm) apart. For reference, a human hair is 80,000 to 100,000 nanometers across. With ASML being the sole supplier of a critical machine in the chip manufacturing world, it has a very solid technological monopoly that will be nearly impossible to break. Taiwan Semiconductor's monopoly status is a bit more shaky but still impressive. There are several other chip foundries out there, and many have the same advanced technology available to make the highest-performance chips possible. However, nobody has the scale that TSMC does. During Q2, Taiwan Semiconductor accounted for about 72.5% of revenue in the chip fabrication industry. That's a major size advantage that holds its clients captive, because they couldn't move all of their work to another foundry if they tried, since its competitors wouldn't have the necessary scale. While this advantage could be challenged over time by a rising competitor, there's nobody even close right now. TSMC has great relationships with its clientele, so I doubt its grip on this industry will be broken anytime over the next decade. While I would say ASML's monopoly status is stronger than TSMC's, I can't say the same about their businesses or stocks.

Lam Research Corporation (NASDAQ:LRCX) reported $2.47 billion of customer-support-related revenue and other in its June quarter. The labels describe different mixtures. ASML and Lam Research both feature in our 10 Best Semiconductor Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade. Both have large businesses supporting equipment already inside chip factories. That can soften a new-equipment slowdown, but calling all of that revenue recurring would give investors too much confidence. Image: Courtesy of ASML ASML defines installed-base management as net service and field-option sales. Its customers need to maintain costly lithography machines, while upgrades can improve their productivity. Yet upgrades remain spending decisions; the entire category should not be treated as an annually contracted subscription. Lam's category combines service, spares, upgrades and non-leading-edge Reliant equipment. That last component is equipment sales. The reported support share therefore cannot establish how much purely recurring service revenue Lam has. Using rounded ASML figures, installed-base sales represented about 28% of quarterly revenue. Lam's broader category represented 36.8%. Assume new-system revenue falls 20% while each support category stays flat. ASML's total sales would decline about 14.4%; Lam's would decline 12.6%. If support revenue also falls 10%, the declines become about 17.2% and 16.3%. Lam's reported mix produces the smaller decline in this exercise, but its equipment content makes a flat support assumption less secure. Neither company discloses enough here to calculate a directly comparable service-only cushion. Lower factory utilization can also reduce demand for spares and usage-related work. ASML benefits from advanced lithography transitions; Lam benefits from increasingly complex deposition and etch processes. Both face export restrictions and delayed customer investments. Our TSMC-ASML cash comparison explains why a strong cash quarter can also reflect payment timing rather than a permanently larger earnings base. At October 16 equity values, trailing cash after capital expenditure cost about 26 times for ASML and 68 times for Lam. Working-capital movements make those historical multiples imperfect measures of sustainable cash; the service-mix exercise cannot justify a stock-price target.

Qualcomm Incorporated QCOM is strengthening its position in the rapidly evolving robotics market through its proposed acquisition of PickNik Robotics, a developer of advanced robotics software. The transaction aligns with Qualcomm's strategy to expand its footprint in physical artificial intelligence (AI), edge computing and intelligent robotics. PickNik is recognized for its stewardship of MoveIt, a widely adopted open-source robotics manipulation framework built on the Robot Operating System (ROS). The platform supports motion planning, manipulation and robotic control across industrial automation, service robotics and emerging physical AI applications. The transaction, subject to customary closing conditions, could strengthen Qualcomm's ability to offer integrated hardware and software solutions. The buyout is expected to enhance Qualcomm's Dragonwing Robotics platforms by integrating MoveIt and PickNik's commercial MoveIt Pro software. This combination could enable developers to leverage Qualcomm's AI processing, connectivity and heterogeneous computing capabilities alongside advanced motion planning and real-time robotic control. The integration is also expected to extend to Arduino platforms, beginning with VENTUNO Q boards. This could make advanced robotics development more accessible to a broader developer community while accelerating the transition from prototypes to commercial deployments. Importantly, Qualcomm intends to maintain MoveIt as an open-source framework supporting third-party hardware. This approach could encourage wider ecosystem participation and strengthen developer engagement, potentially boosting adoption of its Dragonwing platforms. The planned acquisition complements Qualcomm's broader efforts to diversify beyond smartphones into automotive, industrial IoT and edge AI markets. Its March 2026 collaboration with NEURA Robotics to advance cognitive robotics and humanoid applications further underscores its growing focus on physical AI. Combining PickNik's software expertise with Qualcomm's power-efficient computing capabilities could improve its competitive positioning as demand for intelligent automation increases across industrial and commercial applications. However, the acquisition's financial terms remain undisclosed, limiting visibility into its immediate earnings contribution. Integration challenges, competition in robotics computing and uncertain commercialization timelines could also constrain near-term benefits. Stiff competition from NVIDIA Corporation NVDA, Broadcom Inc. AVGO and Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. AMD further strains its margins. Nevertheless, PickNik's established developer ecosystem and robotics software capabilities could help Qualcomm expand its addressable market and deepen customer engagement. Successful integration may strengthen QCOM's position in next-generation robotics while supporting its long-term diversification strategy.

This indicates that the favorable pricing environment that has helped Intel beat Wall Street's earnings per share (EPS) expectations handsomely in each of the last four quarters is sustainable. This insight is at the core of our proprietary surprise prediction model -- the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction). The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a more recent version of the Zacks Consensus EPS estimate. Artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from the chatbots that were popular during the early days of the technology's rollout, when generative AI-based chatbots and assistants, such as ChatGPT, provided a single response to the user's input. AI has now become more capable. Chatbots can perform complex, multi-step tasks to achieve goals by collecting data, using models to break down the objective into steps, and employing external tools such as databases and search engines to provide results. These AI agents can operate autonomously or semi-autonomously to plan tasks and perform actions using software tools. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Not surprisingly, demand for agentic AI is expected to surge due to its benefits. According to a third-party estimate, the agentic AI market could clock a 40% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) over the next seven years, generating $206 billion in revenue in 2033. The agentic AI market's rapid growth has created a surge in demand for server central processing units (CPUs), which explains why Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) and Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) have been enjoying phenomenal growth in their server CPU business. CPUs play a critical role in agentic AI, helping manage the multi-step workflow by coordinating hardware and software resources needed to perform the complex tasks. This is why the ratio of CPUs to GPUs (graphics processing units) in AI servers running agentic AI workloads is shifting from 1:4 earlier to 1:2 or even 1:1, suggesting a 2-4x jump in server CPU demand. AMD and Intel have been winning big from this shift. AMD's data center revenue grew by 107% year over year in the second quarter of 2026. CEO Lisa Su remarked on the recent earnings call: In server, we delivered our fifth consecutive quarter of record server CPU revenue with cloud and enterprise sales each growing more than 70% year-over-year, exceeding the outlook we provided last quarter. Meanwhile, Intel recorded an impressive year-over-year increase of 59% in its data center and AI (DCAI) business in Q2 to $6.3 billion. SMCI's new rack packs 22,528 cores and 45,056 threads, supporting up to 22,500 concurrent agent sandboxes. Sandboxes are isolated computing environments where AI agents can run code, use tools and execute tasks. The system also incorporates Nvidia's BlueField-4 data processing units (DPUs) for networking and security. Supermicro said the rack is available to quote now, while its Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are already shipping. "As enterprises scale agentic AI and reinforcement learning, supporting thousands of concurrent agent workflows requires a new class of high-density CPU infrastructure," said Chris Marriott, vice president of enterprise platforms at Nvidia. The rack also supports Nvidia's OpenShell software, which applies policy-based controls to limit what AI agents can access. Nvidia's Sentry software runs on the BlueField-4 DPUs, monitoring agent activity outside the host CPU and allowing operators to quarantine agents that breach their permissions in milliseconds, according to the release.

CNBC reported that semiconductor equipment maker Lam Research highlighted during its earnings call that shortages of critical upstream parts and certified cleanroom facilities continue to curb manufacturing velocity. As detailed by CNBC, cleanrooms are specialized, dust-free environments essential for fabricating microscopic circuitry without microscopic contaminants damaging delicate silicon wafers. When available cleanroom capacity is restricted, chip fabricators cannot readily install new machinery or ramp up production lines, even when customer appetite for chips remains robust, CNBC explained. Additionally, CNBC noted that lingering supplier bottlenecks mean tool manufacturers struggle to assemble and deliver complex equipment on schedule. While industry leaders are deploying capital to expand production facilities and adjust to evolving structural chip architectures, executive commentary indicates these operational roadblocks will persist into 2027, according to CNBC. As CNBC highlighted, the realization that physical capacity hurdles may cap near-term revenue realization and tool delivery schedules weighed on investor sentiment across the broader semiconductor manufacturing and equipment space. What Does an AI Agent Need a CPU For? Why Nvidia Wants In on the Business Dominated by AMD and Intel

Since the start of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution, the story has centered around the graphics processing unit (GPU). Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) built the world's fastest, and the tech giant's sales skyrocketed. But as AI transitions from answering questions to completing tasks on its own, an...

Since the start of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution, the story has centered around the graphics processing unit (GPU). Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) built the world's fastest, and the tech giant's sales skyrocketed. But as AI transitions from answering questions to completing tasks on its own, another chip is stepping into the spotlight: the central processing unit (CPU). Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) and Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) have long led this market -- but now, Nvidia wants in. Let's consider why AI agents need CPUs and whether Nvidia can dominate in this market too. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » There's been a lot of talk about agentic AI in recent months -- but what exactly is this technology? It's software that works through various steps to reach a particular goal. Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, speaking during an earnings call earlier this year, described an agent as a "harness" built around an AI model, and the harness manages inputs and outputs, memory, tool use, and more. All of that runs on CPUs, while GPUs power the model's "thinking." Huang predicts the world will eventually have billions of AI agents, and all of this should result in more use for GPUs and CPUs. AMD chief executive officer Lisa Su also expects the CPU market to take off. She says CPUs used to be paired with GPUs at a ratio of one to four or one to eight, but that ratio is moving toward one to one, according to TrendForce. AMD now expects server CPU market growth of more than 35% annually, topping $120 billion by 2030, the market intelligence firm added. Nvidia, recognizing the opportunity, is now rolling out the Vera Rubin platform, featuring the company's first stand-alone CPU. Designed specifically for agentic AI, it aims for speed, delivering up to 1.5x faster performance per core compared to CPUs based on x86 architecture, Nvidia says. The tech giant is on track to generate $20 billion in stand-alone CPU revenue this year and says the market opportunity equals $200 billion. Artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from the chatbots that were popular during the early days of the technology's rollout, when generative AI-based chatbots and assistants, such as ChatGPT, provided a single response to the user's input. AI has now become more capable. Chatbots can perform complex, multi-step tasks to achieve goals by collecting data, using models to break down the objective into steps, and employing external tools such as databases and search engines to provide results. These AI agents can operate autonomously or semi-autonomously to plan tasks and perform actions using software tools. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Not surprisingly, demand for agentic AI is expected to surge due to its benefits. According to a third-party estimate, the agentic AI market could clock a 40% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) over the next seven years, generating $206 billion in revenue in 2033. The agentic AI market's rapid growth has created a surge in demand for server central processing units (CPUs), which explains why Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) and Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) have been enjoying phenomenal growth in their server CPU business. CPUs play a critical role in agentic AI, helping manage the multi-step workflow by coordinating hardware and software resources needed to perform the complex tasks. This is why the ratio of CPUs to GPUs (graphics processing units) in AI servers running agentic AI workloads is shifting from 1:4 earlier to 1:2 or even 1:1, suggesting a 2-4x jump in server CPU demand. AMD and Intel have been winning big from this shift. AMD's data center revenue grew by 107% year over year in the second quarter of 2026. CEO Lisa Su remarked on the recent earnings call: In server, we delivered our fifth consecutive quarter of record server CPU revenue with cloud and enterprise sales each growing more than 70% year-over-year, exceeding the outlook we provided last quarter. Meanwhile, Intel recorded an impressive year-over-year increase of 59% in its data center and AI (DCAI) business in Q2 to $6.3 billion. The company believes that its current generation of server CPUs, codenamed Granite Rapids, will help it sustain the impressive growth of the data center business. Intel is ramping up the production of these server CPUs, and it is working with key server OEMs (original equipment manufacturers) such as Dell Technologies, Lenovo, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, and others to bring Granite Rapids to the market.

SMCI's new rack packs 22,528 cores and 45,056 threads, supporting up to 22,500 concurrent agent sandboxes. Sandboxes are isolated computing environments where AI agents can run code, use tools and execute tasks. The system also incorporates Nvidia's BlueField-4 data processing units (DPUs) for networking and security. Supermicro said the rack is available to quote now, while its Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are already shipping. "As enterprises scale agentic AI and reinforcement learning, supporting thousands of concurrent agent workflows requires a new class of high-density CPU infrastructure," said Chris Marriott, vice president of enterprise platforms at Nvidia. The rack also supports Nvidia's OpenShell software, which applies policy-based controls to limit what AI agents can access. Nvidia's Sentry software runs on the BlueField-4 DPUs, monitoring agent activity outside the host CPU and allowing operators to quarantine agents that breach their permissions in milliseconds, according to the release.

Not Nvidia. Not Micron. This Little-Known Chip Stock Is the AI Boom's Best-Kept Secret.

Everyone knows that GPUs are a strong investment because they make an artificial intelligence (AI) data center run, and most investors are now figuring out that memory matters too. What fewer people think about is the cable. Thousands of accelerators in a single building only work if the data between them arrives clean, fast, and without a single dropped link, and the company that has become the reference name for that job is not Nvidia or Micron Technology. It is Credo Technology Group (NASDAQ: CRDO), a connectivity chip designer whose stock has more than tripled in three years and still gets a fraction of the attention its customers give it. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Credo's signature product is something called an active electrical cable, or AEC. It looks like a thick copper cable, but it has Credo's chips built into each end to clean up the signal, allowing hyperscalers to connect servers and switches at 800 gigabits per second over copper instead of paying for power-hungry optical transceivers. The company's purple cables are distinctive enough that Credo trademarked the color. It also sells the retimer and digital signal processor chips inside those cables as stand-alone parts, plus optical DSPs, PCIe retimers, and licensed intellectual property. Credo's "little-known" status is mostly a function of what it sells rather than of how much it sells. Revenue in the quarter ended Aug. 1 more than doubled from a year earlier, and the company has gone from licensing firm to hardware supplier for several of the largest cloud operators in about three years. The reason to pay attention right now is that Credo is in the middle of a planned shift from copper to light, and October is when the pieces showed up. In May, it closed its acquisition of DustPhotonics, an Israeli silicon photonics company, which gave Credo an in-house photonic chip capability to go with its existing DSPs and cable systems. Management said at the time that it expects the combined optical portfolio to become a "significant growth driver" in fiscal 2027. Then at the Open Compute Project summit in San Jose this month, Credo unveiled its 1.6-terabit ZeroFlap Active Light Cable. Instead of pushing a few optical channels to extreme speeds, it uses a dense array of tiny light emitters running in parallel at slower rates. The approach is designed to deliver copper-level reliability out to 50 meters, covering a full row of data center racks, while drawing about 30% less power than a comparable copper AEC and weighing a tenth as much.

Some companies don't keep their ambitions secret. They swagger onto the stock market and draw plenty of attention with a splashy IPO and big promises (lookin' at you, Tesla). But some incredibly successful stocks are sleeper hits: They quietly sit on the market doing nothing until one day, bam! Their shares take off like a rocket, and everybody wonders how they didn't see it coming. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » That's what happened to memory chipmaker Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) in late 2025: Its shares had languished for years until a global memory shortage and AI data center boom took the stock stratospheric. Between June 25, 2025, and June 25, 2026, the chipmaker's shares grew more than 850%. If you were lucky enough to invest $10,000 in Micron on that day in 2025, you'd have had $95,370 a year later. Even today, after shares have dropped 25% from those highs, you'd still have $70,970. Not enough, perhaps, to fund a full retirement, but a nice chunk of change. So, what about right now? Could buying $10,000 in Micron today set you up for life? It's ironic that even though Micron's share price has grown astronomically since June 2025, its price-to-earnings ratio -- how its share price compares to its profits -- has actually gone down. In June 2025, shares were trading at about 22 times earnings. In June 2026, at its peak, it traded at about 27 times earnings. Today, it's trading at about 12 times earnings. Why would a wildly successful company that's grown its revenue by 256% and its per-share earnings by 879% in 16 months have a cheaper valuation than it did before? The simple answer is that the market doesn't expect the good times to last, for two reasons. The first reason is that this has happened before to memory chip stocks, and it didn't end well. Prices for dynamic RAM (DRAM) memory spiked in 2020-2021 during the pandemic tech-buying surge. After expanding capacity to meet that demand, memory producers wound up with a supply glut, and prices crashed in 2023. This time around, Micron has tried to protect itself against such a price crash by signing multiyear supply deals with its customers to lock in price floors, allowing it to safely expand its capacity. That's a smart move, but the market is also concerned about competition.

First, let's talk about Micron's path so far. Though the company opened its doors nearly 50 years ago and has increased revenue over time, revenue truly took off in recent quarters. Memory plays a crucial role in AI from start to finish, meaning it's necessary for the training of models as well as for the application of AI to real-world situations. This use of AI in the real world may be carried out by AI agents, which consider a problem and then take steps to solve it as a human would in the past. They automatically lower the individual price of each share, but they don't change the company's market value or anything fundamental. The process involves offering additional shares to current holders, according to the ratio of the split. So, a person who held one share valued at $1,000, in a 10-for-1 split, would hold 10 shares with the same value following the operation. The motive for such a move is simple: It allows the company to bring its stock to a broader range of potential investors. Some investors can't afford to invest $1,000 and don't have access to fractional shares -- so a stock split gives them the ability to get in on this player that was previously out of reach.

Better Memory Stock: SK Hynix vs. Micron

The memory market is dominated by three large players: pure-play memory makers SK Hynix (NASDAQ: SKHY) and Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU), as well as the conglomerate Samsung. Combined, the three control over 85% of the DRAM (dynamic random-access memory) market and more than 60% of the NAND (flash) market. Soaring demand from the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out has created a significant supply-demand imbalance in the memory market, which in turn has driven surging memory prices. Much of this stems from the need for high bandwidth memory (HBM), a specialized form of DRAM packaged with graphics processing units (GPUs) and other AI accelerators to reduce latency and ensure these expensive chips aren't left idle due to memory bottlenecks. Demand for HBM is growing in lockstep with demand for compute power, leading the big three memory makers to concentrate their resources on HBM. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » However, the ability to increase HBM capacity is limited. ASML is the only company in the world that makes the extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines needed to manufacture critical HBM components. Meanwhile, these are the same systems needed to make GPUs and other advanced logic chips. With foundries and memory makers competing for a limited number of new EUV machines, they are unable to keep up with demand. On top of that, HBM requires roughly three times the wafer capacity as ordinary DRAM, adding to the constraints. With the big three memory makers focused on increasing HBM capacity, the supply-demand balance has also spread to conventional DRAM and NAND. NAND, meanwhile, is seeing huge demand come from the need for massive solid-state drives (SSDs) that store AI training data. As a result, conventional NAND and DRAM prices have risen faster than HBM prices. This is important when comparing SK Hynix and Micron and determining which looks like the better AI stock to own. SK Hynix is the market leader in HBM and the memory maker that derives the largest percentage of its revenue from advanced memory. In Q2, it held a 25% share of the DRAM market and a 50% share of the HBM market. It also held a 19% share of the NAND market. The company is the main HBM supplier to Nvidia, and the two companies have a partnership in which Nvidia has locked up $500 billion in future memory commitments.

Micron Technology Inc (NASDAQ:MU)'s decision to bypass 4F² DRAM architecture in favour of 3D technology could help it maintain its competitive edge, according to Wedbush, which sees the chipmaker's manufacturing progress as a key strength. In a technology update, Micron outlined its product roadmap and explained why it has no plans to adopt 4F², a memory cell design intended to increase DRAM density. Micron sees two fundamental limitations with the approach, Wedbush said. The technology has no clear path to further scaling beyond a certain point, while capacitor pitch, rather than cell layout, ultimately determines memory density. Micron also believes 4F² was more complex and costly to implement even on earlier process nodes. Wedbush said Micron's execution over the past decade supports its technology strategy, noting that the company has progressed from lagging Asian competitors to producing DRAM and NAND products that are arguably among the industry's best. The analysts highlighted Micron's early adoption of CMOS under the array for NAND manufacturing and its subsequent shift to extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography as examples of its ability to navigate different technology paths. In DRAM, Wedbush believes Micron is furthest along in transitioning manufacturing to its 1c process node. Its planned transition to the 1-delta process node in the second half of 2027 also appears to position it to remain ahead in industry node transitions. The assessment has implications for China's memory ambitions. Wedbush suggested that Chinese manufacturers could be pursuing alternative approaches to compensate for their technology disadvantages and limited access to EUV equipment. While the analysts continue to view China's DRAM industry as the biggest longer-term risk to market conditions, they said the greater concern is the country's access to capital and potential production volumes, rather than technological innovation. That could leave memory supply and pricing vulnerable to expanding Chinese output, even if domestic manufacturers struggle to match the most advanced technologies. Shares of Micron were down around 5.6% on Thursday.

This has supercharged earnings growth, and the stock price has taken off as investors recognized this company's position in a high-potential market. The AI market is expected to soar into the trillions by the early 2030s, and Micron is well placed to benefit. Still, the stock has advanced more than 1,000% over three years, and in 2026 it's heading for a gain of more than 200%. With this in mind, you may be wondering if there's much fuel left in the tank. Is Micron a millionaire-maker stock after its 2026 run? Let's find out. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » First, let's consider Micron's path so far. This tech giant has been around for decades, serving the needs of tech companies with its products. This market has always been cyclical, with memory chip demand ebbing and flowing over the years. That has resulted in some dips and peaks in revenue, but over time, this tech giant has grown its relationships with customers and its earnings. So, it's a well-established memory player that investors can count on over time -- even if demand slows on occasion, this pattern is expected. MU Revenue (Annual) data by YCharts The AI boom represented a fresh growth opportunity for Micron. The company's memory chips have been useful throughout the AI story, as memory and storage are needed for model training as well as the application of AI to real-world problems. But revenue growth truly took off in recent quarters as the agentic AI opportunity emerged. Agentic AI involves AI addressing an issue on behalf of a human and taking various steps to complete tasks. This represents an almost limitless opportunity for memory and storage companies, as these chips are needed on an ongoing basis for AI agents to operate. By comparison, training needs the memory capacity once, as the training is happening. So agentic AI represents a much bigger growth opportunity for memory makers like Micron. This is great news, because agentic AI is expected to be used more and more as AI is applied in the real world.

Taiwan Semiconductor and ASML Are Incredible, but 1 of These Monopoly Chip Stocks Is Far Safer.

No summary available

There are few companies on the market more impressive than Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM) and ASML Holding (NASDAQ: ASML). Both are essentially monopolies for different reasons, but each is an incredible business and has rewarded shareholders with strong stock performance. However, ...

There are few companies on the market more impressive than Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM) and ASML Holding (NASDAQ: ASML). Both are essentially monopolies for different reasons, but each is an incredible business and has rewarded shareholders with strong stock performance. However, these two aren't the same from an investment standpoint. One is far safer, and it all boils down to how much success is priced into the stock. I think Taiwan Semiconductor is the far safer bet for multiple reasons, making it the better investment right now. Here's why. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » There are different types of monopolies, and not all of them are viewed the same way. When it comes to monopolies, ASML is about as good as it gets. It is the only company in the world with the technology to make extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. These machines are about as big as a school bus and cost hundreds of millions of dollars. EUV machines are used by chip fabricators, such as Taiwan Semiconductor, to lay down tiny electrical traces on chips. These traces are microscopic and have spacing as little as 2 nanometers (nm) apart. For reference, a human hair is 80,000 to 100,000 nanometers across. With ASML being the sole supplier of a critical machine in the chip manufacturing world, it has a very solid technological monopoly that will be nearly impossible to break. Taiwan Semiconductor's monopoly status is a bit more shaky but still impressive. There are several other chip foundries out there, and many have the same advanced technology available to make the highest-performance chips possible. However, nobody has the scale that TSMC does. During Q2, Taiwan Semiconductor accounted for about 72.5% of revenue in the chip fabrication industry. That's a major size advantage that holds its clients captive, because they couldn't move all of their work to another foundry if they tried, since its competitors wouldn't have the necessary scale. While this advantage could be challenged over time by a rising competitor, there's nobody even close right now. TSMC has great relationships with its clientele, so I doubt its grip on this industry will be broken anytime over the next decade. While I would say ASML's monopoly status is stronger than TSMC's, I can't say the same about their businesses or stocks.

TSMC reported Q3 revenue of $46.72 billion, a 41.2% increase from a year ago. Net income jumped 68.7%, while the company's gross profit margin reached 66.4%. Those are impressive numbers by any measure, particularly for a company of TSMC's size. But there's another figure buried in the company's earnings presentation that I think is even more important. High-performance computing (HPC) accounted for a whopping 68% of TSMC's quarterly revenue, with sales in that business increasing 22% from Q2. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » That tells us quite a bit about where TSMC's growth is coming from -- and why its artificial intelligence (AI) business remains such an important opportunity for investors. TSMC is the biggest chip foundry in the world, manufacturing chips for companies such as Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, and Apple. TSMC has an overwhelming 72.5% of the global market share and, in 2025, produced more than 12,600 products using 305 separate process technologies. That business model gives TSMC an interesting advantage. It doesn't necessarily have to predict which chip designer will come out on top because it can manufacture chips for competing companies. And increasingly, those chips are being used for high-performance computing. HPC includes processors used in AI accelerators, data centers, and other demanding computing applications. It's a broader category than artificial intelligence alone, but AI is an important driver of demand for the advanced chips that TSMC manufactures. In Q3, HPC generated more than two-thirds of the company's revenue compared with just 21% from smartphones. And while TSMC's overall revenue increased 16.2% sequentially, HPC revenue grew even faster at 22%. The growth also comes as major technology companies continue investing in the computing infrastructure needed to train and operate increasingly powerful AI models. Those investments create demand for advanced processors, and TSMC manufactures many of the chips used in those systems. The power of a changing earnings picture in determining near-term stock price movements makes the Zacks rating system highly useful for individual investors, since it can be difficult to make decisions based on rating upgrades by Wall Street analysts. An increase or decrease in earnings estimates in their valuation models simply results in higher or lower fair value for a stock, and institutional investors typically buy or sell it. Their transaction of large amounts of shares then leads to price movement for the stock. Fundamentally speaking, rising earnings estimates and the consequent rating upgrade for TSMC imply an improvement in the company's underlying business. Taiwan's Stock Pickers Are Walking Out to Bet Their Own Money

NEW YORK, Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fly On Wall Street News Commentary - Taiwan's benchmark stock index was up 62% this year, the best showing of any major equity gauge in the world, when Bloomberg reported on Oct. 16 that some of the island's professional fund managers and analysts are quitting their jobs to invest their own money. Strict rules keep them from trading the very stocks they pick for clients, and in a year when about one in ten stocks in the index has more than doubled, some have decided the trade-off is no longer worth it. Companies and funds mentioned in this article include: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited [TSMC] (NYSE: TSM), ASE Technology Holding Co., Ltd. [ASE] (NYSE: ASX), United Microelectronics Corporation [UMC] (NYSE: UMC), iShares MSCI Taiwan ETF (NYSE Arca: EWT), The Taiwan Fund, Inc. (NYSE: TWN). Watching From Behind the Locker Taiwan does not ban personal investing outright, but its asset-management code of conduct bars staff from trading a locally listed stock or a linked derivative within seven business days before or after their firm's funds trade it, which in practice rules out personal stock-picking. Fund managers must also lock away their phones, laptops and smartwatches each morning until the market closes at 1:30 p.m. The phone rule was formalized in 2024 to deter insider trading, the Taipei Times reported in July, after six former fund managers from four firms were indicted for front-running trades through the accounts of relatives and friends. Ken Tsai, 40, a fund manager who until July worked at a large Taiwanese asset manager that Bloomberg did not name, told Bloomberg he made a Taiwanese maker of AI-server data-transfer components his fund's largest holding in 2024. The stock rose more than fivefold in 2025 and about sixfold again this year, but he owned none of it personally. "It left me with a strong sense of relative deprivation," he said. He now works at a private investment firm in Taipei, which was also not named. Pay adds to the pull: Taiwan portfolio managers earn roughly US$124,000 to US$311,000 a year, well below Hong Kong base salaries, according to Bloomberg, citing headhunters and recruitment-firm data. The private shops they are joining sit outside those rules. They register as private companies with the Ministry of Economic Affairs and do not need asset-management licenses from the Financial Supervisory Commission because they do not raise public money. Brokers told Bloomberg some of them now generate more than NT$10 billion in monthly trading volume, rivaling mid-sized asset managers.

Broadcom Launches Arcot Scam Defense to Block Social Engineering Fraud

No summary available

PALO ALTO, Calif., Oct. 21, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ: AVGO), a global technology leader that designs, develops, and supplies semiconductors and infrastructure software, today announced the launch of Arcot Scam Defense, a groundbreaking new feature of Arcot by Broadcom, designed...

PALO ALTO, Calif., Oct. 21, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ: AVGO), a global technology leader that designs, develops, and supplies semiconductors and infrastructure software, today announced the launch of Arcot Scam Defense, a groundbreaking new feature of Arcot by Broadcom, designed to block social engineering fraud during card-not-present (CNP) transactions. "Financial institutions are experiencing broad increases in fraud attempts driven by sophisticated, AI-enhanced social engineering attacks," said Matt Cooke, vice president and general manager, Payment Security Division, Broadcom. "While technological security systems have advanced and are highly effective at blocking fraud, fraudsters have pivoted their efforts to hacking customers directly. By impersonating trusted brands and institutions, they trick cardholders into revealing passwords or completing step-up authentications. Cardholders usually remain unaware that they have handed over the keys to the castle until after the scam." How Social Engineering Works During a payment flow, once a cardholder completes a 3-D Secure authentication challenge, by entering a one-time password (OTP) or using a biometric, the transaction is treated as legitimate and is approved by a financial institution's primary risk models. While real-time risk assessment models are highly effective at flagging suspicious transactions, they are not designed to stop a legitimate account holder actively under the influence of a scam. Introducing Arcot Scam Defense "Arcot Scam Defense closes a critical gap," added Cooke. "It serves as the definitive safety net against social engineering attacks. Operating as a real-time second layer of defense, it leverages advanced intelligence during authentication to flag suspected fraud – even after a successful challenge. By closing the approval door on these attacks, we increase cardholder safety and drive down fraud losses, while continuing to allow legitimate transactions through." Arcot Scam Defense analyzes a broad range of signals across transaction information, device intelligence, historical behavior, and the challenge interaction itself to identify patterns indicative of social engineering. These can include discrepancies in the location and behavior of the transacting checkout device and the authenticating device, delayed OTP entry, the use of an alternative authentication method, or a significant physical distance between the two devices. These signals are evaluated collectively to inform a real-time decision rather than relying on any single indicator. Additionally, the solution can integrate with third-party solutions to determine if the authenticating device is on an active phone call, which is a prime indicator of social engineering.

The carrier said its contract gave it the option to renew support for two more years. Broadcom would only continue supporting AT&T through new subscription packages requiring three-year contracts, AT&T alleged. At a hearing on Oct. 23, 2024, AT&T's lawyer said the carrier would seek to leave VMware over licensing and cost changes. "Without the threat, there's really no way Broadcom will become more reasonable," he told the court. The two sides reported a settlement in principle that December, without disclosing terms. Now another telecom giant is heading the other way. NTT DOCOMO, the mobile arm of Japan's NTT, has signed a 10-year deal to keep its private cloud on VMware Cloud Foundation, according to a Broadcom press release on Oct. 19, 2026. The length is the surprise. Forrester analyst Naveen Chhabra told TechTarget that most customers would sooner reduce their VMware dependence over time than fight. DOCOMO just committed for a decade. DOCOMO is taking Cloud Foundation plus VMware's load balancing, vDefend security, and its Tanzu app platform. It also gets dedicated account managers and VCF Forte Support, which carries Broadcom's strictest service targets. To me, that reads like the showcase Broadcom has wanted since it folded VMware's catalog into two main bundles, as TechTarget confirmed. The container piece matters more than it looks. DOCOMO will run virtual machines and containers on one platform using VMware's own Kubernetes service, according to the release. A carrier modernizing its software could have used that shift to walk away, and DOCOMO chose to stay. AT&T's lawsuit leaned on one warning. Its lawyers argued that losing VMware support could knock out vital systems for public safety agencies, according to TechTarget. VMware, in other words, was too embedded to unplug quickly. DOCOMO's priorities read as that same worry turned into a purchase. The carrier wants to upgrade systems without interruptions and hold quality steady through traffic spikes. "VMware products have long been used across a range of our systems," said Hiroshi Ishimaru, a DOCOMO general manager, in the release.

About the Industry The Zacks Alternative Energy - Other industry can be fundamentally segregated into two sets of companies. Such investments provide strong growth opportunities for industry participants. 3 Trends Shaping the Future of the Alternative Energy Industry Wind Power Market Poised for Sustained Growth: The global wind power market continues to expand, driven by supportive government policies for renewable energy, rising focus on decarbonization and energy security, and improving cost competitiveness. Technological advancements, particularly the development of larger and more efficient turbines, are helping wind farms generate more electricity from existing sites while reducing production costs and enhancing project profitability. These factors are expected to drive sustained growth in the industry over the long term. Higher Interest Rates Pose Challenges for Alternative Energy Growth: The Federal Reserve's September 2026 interest rate hike, which raised the federal fund target range to 3.75-4.00%, has increased financing concerns for the alternative energy sector. Since renewable energy projects require substantial upfront capital and often depend on debt financing, higher borrowing costs can weaken project economics, pressure profit margins and delay new investments. Capital-intensive technologies such as offshore wind, carbon capture and low-carbon hydrogen may face greater challenges due to their financial and execution risks. The smaller the standard deviation, the greater the agreement among analysts. While the consensus price target is a much-coveted metric for investors, solely banking on this metric to make an investment decision may not be wise at all. That's because the ability and unbiasedness of analysts in setting price targets have long been questionable. But, for CEG, an impressive average price target is not the only indicator of a potential upside. Strong agreement among analysts about the company's ability to report better earnings than they predicted earlier strengthens this view. While a positive trend in earnings estimate revisions doesn't gauge how much a stock could gain, it has proven to be powerful in predicting an upside. According to researchers at several universities across the globe, a price target is one of many pieces of information about a stock that misleads investors far more often than it guides. In fact, empirical research shows that price targets set by several analysts, irrespective of the extent of agreement, rarely indicate where the price of a stock could actually be heading. While Wall Street analysts have deep knowledge of a company's fundamentals and the sensitivity of its business to economic and industry issues, many of them tend to set overly optimistic price targets. Are you wondering why? They usually do that to drum up interest in shares of companies that their firms either have existing business relationships with or are looking to be associated with. In other words, business incentives of firms covering a stock often result in inflated price targets set by analysts. However, a tight clustering of price targets, which is represented by a low standard deviation, indicates that analysts have a high degree of agreement about the direction and magnitude of a stock's price movement. While that doesn't necessarily mean the stock will hit the average price target, it could be a good starting point for further research aimed at identifying the potential fundamental driving forces.

The technology sector's commitment to nuclear energy continues to strengthen. Just last week, Google's parent company Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) agreed to purchase nuclear-generated electricity from utility company Constellation Energy's (NASDAQ: CEG) existing nuclear power plants for 15 years, in addition to making a 20-year agreement to purchase 890 megawatts' worth of power from nuclear power production facilities that Constellation will build in the future. Alphabet's long-term commitment will enable Constellation Energy to confidently invest $4.3 billion in new nuclear energy capacity, adding to its already-extensive nuclear power portfolio. Constellation shares jumped on the news, of course. But so did shares of small modular reactor (SMR) developers Oklo (NYSE: OKLO) and NuScale (NYSE: SMR), despite having no involvement in Constellation's agreement with Google. What gives? Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » NuScale and Oklo may be positioned to enter the nuclear energy business. However, they're not like Constellation. Constellation Energy's typical nuclear power facility is built to serve hundreds of thousands of utility customers. NuScale and Oklo, on the other hand, are working on small-scale reactors designed to power facilities such as refineries, smelters, and desalination plants, built where the electricity is consumed. The two approaches to providing power are obviously very different -- different enough that investors seemingly shouldn't conflate the two. Yet, they did. Why? Because there's a more philosophical message being delivered here. That's the general recognition that nuclear energy is a far more practical solution to the growing power shortage that renewables were expected to shore up by now. Alphabet's management may not be interested in small modular nuclear reactors (yet). Other companies could be, given the broader reacceptance of this once-waning energy source. Investors are simply connecting the dots, and reasonably so. SMRs will never account for the lion's share of the planet's nuclear power generation, to be clear. Their fiscal math just doesn't make sense at scale. Nevertheless, when grid independence is necessary and desirable, and the need is modest, they do have their place. That's why there are now over 70 small modular reactors already planned, if not already being built, according to estimates from the World Nuclear Association, compared to none in true commercial operation.

Centrus Energy Corp. (NYSE:LEU) announced the acquisition of Westerman Holdings for approximately $116 million, as the nuclear fuel supplier seeks to expand its manufacturing capabilities and secure components required for its uranium enrichment operations. The transaction was financed through approximately $95 million in cash and $21 million in equity. Centrus shares advanced following the announcement, although the company did not provide a specific percentage movement in the information released. The acquisition brings an existing supplier of centrifuge components under Centrus's ownership and adds manufacturing operations serving the nuclear, oil and gas, and broader industrial sectors. Centrus expects the transaction to contribute positively to adjusted earnings per share during the first year following completion. Westerman Holdings currently manufactures centrifuge casings and other major components used in Centrus's uranium enrichment operations. By acquiring the company, Centrus intends to integrate a portion of its manufacturing supply chain and increase control over the production of equipment required for its planned capacity expansion. Centrifuges are used in uranium enrichment to separate uranium isotopes, a process that produces fuel suitable for use in commercial nuclear reactors. Manufacturing the specialised components required for these systems is an important part of developing and maintaining enrichment capacity. Centrus said the acquisition would support its ability to obtain these components as it expands production. The company also expects the integration to reduce certain project costs and improve operational efficiency. However, it did not disclose specific cost-saving targets or a timetable for achieving the anticipated efficiencies. The acquisition forms part of Centrus's previously announced multibillion-dollar programme to expand uranium enrichment capacity. The company is investing in manufacturing and production capabilities intended to support the development of additional enrichment infrastructure. Westerman's existing relationship with Centrus means the acquired business already produces components used in the company's centrifuge systems. Bringing these activities under common ownership is intended to provide greater coordination between equipment manufacturing and enrichment capacity development. Centrus expects the transaction to improve supply chain integration as it progresses with its expansion plans.

Centrus Acquires Westerman Holdings, LLC, Bringing a Key Supplier In-House and Diversifying Its Manufacturing Capacity

No summary available

Secures a key centrifuge component supplier and best-in-class manufacturer with an existing and growing business Diversifies revenue base by expanding Centrus' addressable market with significant adjacent, non-nuclear manufacturing work Drives continued growth for both organizations through commer...

Secures a key centrifuge component supplier and best-in-class manufacturer with an existing and growing business Diversifies revenue base by expanding Centrus' addressable market with significant adjacent, non-nuclear manufacturing work Drives continued growth for both organizations through commercial and operational synergies and cost savings BETHESDA, Md., Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Centrus Energy Corp. (NYSE: LEU) ("Centrus"), a trusted supplier of nuclear fuel and services, today announced that it has acquired Westerman Holdings, LLC ("Westerman"), one of Centrus' largest and most diversified suppliers, for approximately $116 million, funded through a combination of approximately $95 million cash on hand and $21 million of equity. The transaction is expected to be accretive to adjusted earnings per share in the first year following closing. The acquisition represents a significant milestone for Centrus as it builds supply chain resilience while diversifying its revenue base. Westerman's expertise strengthens and de-risks Centrus' supply chain by securing and bringing in-house its critical manufacturing capabilities. The acquisition simultaneously broadens Centrus' manufacturing platform, customer base, and future revenue opportunities through commercial and operational synergies. The addition of Westerman supports Centrus' previously announced multi-billion-dollar expansion of uranium enrichment capacity. Westerman is an existing manufacturer for centrifuge casings and other major centrifuge components for Centrus. With the acquisition, Centrus intends to secure this key supplier while expanding Westerman's capabilities. Westerman currently services a number of non-nuclear customers across a variety of industries including oil and gas as well as other high-growth industrial sectors, diversifying Centrus' revenue base beyond its core nuclear business. The acquisition is expected to result in lower project costs for Centrus and greater efficiencies with an integrated supply chain. "Westerman is a highly regarded, best-in-class supplier and fabricator for Centrus, the broader nuclear industry, and a number of other sectors," said Amir Vexler, President and CEO of Centrus. "Bringing Westerman in-house demonstrates our commitment to securing our supply chain to support our build-out while adding to our capabilities and expanding our customer base. We are committed to growing and expanding Westerman alongside our enrichment business, and are confident that this transaction will unlock significant value for our shareholders."

That's where Centrus Energy (NYSE: LEU) sees its opportunity. The company already supplies low-enriched uranium (LEU) to nuclear power operators, but its biggest growth opportunity could come from high-assay, low-enriched uranium (HALEU). Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Becoming a leading U.S. producer of this next-generation fuel could make Centrus the ultimate pick-and-shovel play on the nuclear technology boom. Here's what investors need to know. Centrus is an important player in the U.S. nuclear fuel supply chain. Currently, the company generates most of its revenue from supplying LEU to utilities operating traditional nuclear reactors in the U.S. and abroad. The company has manufacturing capabilities, but over the last decade, it has sourced this fuel globally, making it an established middleman. However, this is all changing. In 2023, Congress passed the Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act, which blocks the import of natural uranium and LEU produced in Russia or by a Russian entity. Some operators have been given limited waivers to import from Russia, but these waivers are set to expire on Jan. 1, 2028. The restrictions will remain in place until Dec. 31, 2040. Centrus relies heavily on TENEX, a Russian state-owned entity, for its LEU. Over half of the LEU it delivers to customers in 2027 is expected to come from TENEX. Russia holds roughly 43% of global enrichment capacity, so Congress' act creates an urgent need to develop domestic nuclear fuel production. The company is pivoting from being an intermediary to becoming a U.S. producer of these fuels. It is making a multibillion-dollar investment in its Ohio and Tennessee facilities to expand domestic enrichment capacity. In Oak Ridge, Tennessee, management is investing over $560 million to produce thousands of centrifuges. Meanwhile, it's expanding its Piketon, Ohio, centrifuge and enrichment plant to develop LEU and HALEU at scale.

The company is pioneering HALEU production at its enrichment facility in Ohio, the only licensed HALEU production facility in the Western world. Notably, around $2.4 billion of these commitments are under definitive agreements, increasing confidence that portions of the backlog can eventually translate into material revenue. Production will be "unobligated" that can support national security missions Adds another HALEU customer to Centrus' backlog and includes prepayments to advance domestic enrichment capacity buildout BETHESDA, Md. and TORRANCE, Calif., Sept. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Centrus Energy (NYSE: LEU) and Antares Nuclear today announced the signing of a definitive multi-year contract for Centrus to supply Antares with High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU), with deliveries commencing before the end of the decade. It ensures a reliable, domestic source of HALEU to support Antares advanced reactor projects, including for space and national security missions. The new contract includes prepayments from Antares to support the expanded HALEU capacity. "This contract is another sign that demand for HALEU is real and it is accelerating, and Centrus is in prime position to meet this need," said Amir Vexler, President and CEO of Centrus. "Binding orders from Antares and others are supporting our expansion to commercial-scale production – an expansion that is now well underway. We look forward to supporting Antares' continued growth and success." "Fuel supply is one of the practical questions every advanced reactor developer has to answer," said Jordan Bramble, CEO and Co-Founder of Antares. "This contract gives Antares a reliable, U.S.-origin source of HALEU for the reactors we're deploying for a wide variety of defense and space customers." Antares is developing compact microreactors for critical missions on Earth and in space. The company was recently selected for the U.S. Army's Janus Program at Fort Bragg, North Carolina; the Air Force's Advanced Nuclear Power for Installations program at Joint Base San Antonio, Texas; and a Space Force Strategic Breakthrough award to demonstrate a space reactor. Centrus is pioneering U.S. HALEU production at its American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio, the only licensed HALEU production facility in the western world. Last year, Centrus launched a multi-billion-dollar expansion including large-scale production of HALEU as well as Low-Enriched Uranium (LEU). The agreement reflects the unique role that both companies can play in meeting U.S. national security requirements. Because Centrus's enrichment technology and manufacturing supply chain are U.S.-origin, the arrangement can provide Antares with fuel that could be used for a variety of national security applications. Centrus' AC100 centrifuge design is the only deployment-ready enrichment technology capable of "unobligated" enrichment, meaning that it can be used for U.S. national security missions.

Centrus Announces Pricing of $500 Million Underwritten Public Offering of Class A Common Stock and Warrants

No summary available

BETHESDA, Md., Sept. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Centrus Energy Corp. (NYSE: LEU) ("Centrus" or the "Company") today announced the pricing of its previously announced underwritten public offering of 500,000 shares of its Class A common stock (the "Class A Common Stock"), pre-funded warrants (the "Pre-Fu...

BETHESDA, Md., Sept. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Centrus Energy Corp. (NYSE: LEU) ("Centrus" or the "Company") today announced the pricing of its previously announced underwritten public offering of 500,000 shares of its Class A common stock (the "Class A Common Stock"), pre-funded warrants (the "Pre-Funded Warrants") to purchase an aggregate of 2,005,513 shares of Class A Common Stock and common warrants (the "Common Warrants") to purchase up to an aggregate of 6,992,382 shares of Class A Common Stock. The offering is priced at a combined public offering price of $199.64 per share of Class A Common Stock and accompanying Common Warrants and $199.54 per Pre-Funded Warrant and accompanying Common Warrants. The purchase price of each Pre-Funded Warrant is equal to the price per share at which shares of Class A Common Stock are being sold in the offering, minus the exercise price for the Pre-Funded Warrants of $0.10 per share. Investors purchasing shares of Class A Common Stock or Pre-Funded Warrants will also receive a pro rata allocation of Common Warrants based on the number of shares of Class A Common Stock or Pre-Funded Warrants purchased by that investor. The closing of the offering is expected to occur on or about September 11, 2026, subject to the satisfaction of customary closing conditions. The Pre-Funded Warrants will be immediately exercisable upon issuance for an aggregate of 2,005,513 shares of Class A Common Stock at a nominal exercise price of $0.10 per share. The Common Warrants will be immediately exercisable from the date of issuance for an aggregate of 6,992,382 shares of Class A Common Stock. The Common Warrants will be issued in four series, each with an aggregate exercise price of approximately $500 million. The exercise price for each series will equal $226.8625, $272.2350, $317.6075, and $362.9800 per share of the Class A Common Stock, respectively. Each series will be divided into two equal tranches. The first tranche will expire on the second, third, fourth or fifth anniversary of September 10, 2026, as applicable, and the second tranche will expire on the date that is nine weeks after each such anniversary. The gross proceeds from the offering are expected to be approximately $500 million, before deducting the underwriting discount and other estimated offering expenses payable by Centrus. The gross proceeds from the offering do not include any proceeds that may be received upon exercise of the Common Warrants. The Company intends to use the net proceeds from the offering for general working capital and corporate purposes, which may include investment in technology development and deployment, repayment or repurchase of outstanding debt, capital expenditures, potential acquisitions and other business opportunities and purposes.

In the Permian, the integrated giant has been employing new drilling techniques and artificial intelligence to boost and optimize production volumes at lower cost structures. In Guyana, XOM has made several oil and gas discoveries, further highlighting its solid production outlook. Robust production from both assets has been aiding its top and bottom lines. Breakeven costs are low in both resources. Turning to BP, the British energy major's production outlook looks bright, as its major projects, expected to begin operations between 2028 and 2030, are moving forward as planned. Once operational, these projects could help BP increase production and generate more cash. Although high oil prices are acting as a tailwind for the businesses of XOM and BP, it is also necessary to analyze the companies' financial strength to judge how well the two energy majors could weather an unfavorable commodity pricing environment. The debt-to-capitalization of XOM is 13.73%, much lower than BP's 43.29%. Thus, with significantly lower exposure to debt capital, ExxonMobil Holdings can sail through a tough business environment. Exxon just showed why gas prices didn't fall with oil

No summary available

There's a quiet rule in household budgeting. The bills that hurt most are the ones you can't negotiate. You can shop around for car insurance and switch phone plans. You can't haggle at the pump. For most of 2026, that rule has been expensive. Last month was the priciest September on record for ga...

There's a quiet rule in household budgeting. The bills that hurt most are the ones you can't negotiate. You can shop around for car insurance and switch phone plans. You can't haggle at the pump. For most of 2026, that rule has been expensive. Last month was the priciest September on record for gasoline, with the monthly national average landing at $4.33 a gallon, 50 cents above the prior September high, according to AAA. By Oct. 17, the national average was still about $4.31 a gallon, AAA noted. Here's the part that should really bother you. Crude oil, the raw ingredient in every gallon, got cheaper over the summer. The average Brent closing price fell about 5.6% in the third quarter from the second, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters. So where did that relief go? ExxonMobil just answered the question in a regulatory filing. The company said on Oct. 16 that higher refining margins could add $4.5 billion to third-quarter earnings in its Energy Products segment compared with the second quarter, according to its Form 8-K filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Exxon plans to post full third-quarter results at about 5:30 a.m. Central time on Oct. 30. The 8-K isn't an earnings forecast, and Exxon says so plainly. It's a list of market and planned factors management expects to move results from one quarter to the next. The numbers still tell a clear story. Here's how the biggest pieces stack up against the second quarter, according to the filing: Refining margins in Energy Products: +$4.5 billion Specialty Products margins: +$500 million Chemical Products margins: -$600 million Lower crude and liquids prices in Upstream: -$1.3 billion Natural gas prices: +$300 million Lighter scheduled maintenance: +$200 million Estimated timing effects: -$2.5 billion, which Exxon strips out of adjusted earnings In my read of that table, the oil-pumping side of Exxon lost $1.3 billion to cheaper crude, while the fuel-making side picked up more than three times that amount. Analysts expect Exxon's third-quarter refining earnings to land near $7.8 billion, which would be a company record, according to Bloomberg. BMO Capital Markets analyst Phillip Jungwirth went higher, writing that refining adjusted net income could reach $8.5 billion, Reuters reported. Either figure would roughly double the $4.1 billion the refining business earned in the second quarter. A refining margin is the gap between what a refiner pays for crude and what it gets for gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. When that gap widens, refiners win, and drivers cover the difference.

ExxonMobil (XOM:NYSE) told investors on Friday, October 16, that higher refining margins could add $4.5 billion to third-quarter profit in its Energy Products business compared with the second quarter, according to a regulatory filing. The stock closed up 2.5% at $178.98, a record close. One caveat before the numbers. The $4.5 billion is the effect of refining margins alone, measured at second-quarter volumes. It isn't a forecast of Exxon's total profit, and the filing says so. Full results arrive on October 30. Energy Products, the segment that holds Exxon's refineries, earned $4.1 billion on an adjusted basis in the second quarter, and the margin gain comes on top of that. Add the segment's smaller items (lighter maintenance and extra days, minus $400 million of external disruptions) and BMO Capital Markets analyst Phillip Jungwirth puts adjusted refining profit near $8.5 billion. That's more than double the second quarter. The rest of the filing pulls the other way. Lower crude prices take $1.3 billion out of Upstream, weaker chemical margins cost $600 million, and $2.5 billion of derivative timing effects will hit reported earnings before unwinding in later quarters. Energy Products revenue fell from $371.87 billion in 2022 to $290.32 billion in 2025, a 22% drop, and the segment reported $7.4 billion of earnings last year. Jungwirth's roughly $8.5 billion for the third quarter alone is an adjusted figure, so the two aren't a clean match. The $4.5 billion is a pure margin effect, calculated at second-quarter volumes, and actual volumes arrive with the October 30 results. That per-barrel profit comes from a fuel shortage. CEO Darren Woods has argued that pump prices are now set by scarce refining capacity rather than crude, a point TIKR covered in August. The peers show the same thing. Shell (SHEL) put its indicative refining margin at $42 a barrel, up from $24. TotalEnergies (TTE) saw its European margin rise to $33.2 from $13.5. BP (BP) expects stronger refining margins to add $1.9 billion to $2.1 billion. Analysts expect Exxon's normalized EPS to nearly double, from $6.99 in 2025 to $12.94 in 2026, then slip to $11.86 in 2027. That's a drop of about 8%, so analysts expect most of this year's earnings jump to carry into 2027. Those are companywide estimates that also reflect oil prices, production and buybacks, but refining is the piece that moved most this year.
