Factories need heat to refine crude oil, produce chemicals and manufacture fertilizers, with much of that energy coming from fossil fuels. According to a U.S. Department of Energy analysis cited by NuScale, process heating accounted for 51% of manufacturing energy use in 2018. NuScale says a plant with 12 Power Modules could supply 3 gigawatts of thermal energy as superheated steam. This could give industrial customers another way to meet their heat needs while reducing emissions. Industrial facilities need steam at specific temperatures and pressures, making it difficult to replace conventional boilers. NuScale has been studying how its reactors could meet those requirements. In a 2025 assessment published with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, several proposed systems were found capable of serving a large chemical facility while potentially cutting carbon dioxide emissions by 80% to 90%. NuScale is also working with Ebara Elliott Energy on a high-temperature steam compressor. The planned system would use equipment to raise reactor-supplied steam to 500°C or more, making it suitable for additional industrial uses. These projects could open another market for NuScale, although commercial adoption remains uncertain. Its reactor design supports an emergency planning zone at the plant boundary, allowing installations closer to factories and reducing heat lost during transport. The company has studied ways to supply electricity and steam for hydrogen and ammonia production. However, these studies do not amount to industrial sales. NuScale must demonstrate its systems at commercial scale, secure customers and arrange financing before process heat can become a revenue source. Successful projects could improve the business outlook for SMR stock. NuScale is not alone in exploring nuclear energy for industrial heat applications. Other advanced nuclear developers are also working on smaller reactor designs that could supply both electricity and heat to industrial facilities. As industries look for ways to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels, demand for such technologies could increase, creating new business opportunities while intensifying competition in the nuclear energy market. Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » At this price, most of what a buyer pays for every share is cash. To me, that's the biggest shift in this stock over the last year. A stock trading so close to its cash can look like a value stock. But it isn't necessarily cheap when the company keeps selling new shares to refill the cash. Image source: Getty Images. As of June 30, 2026, NuScale's cash, cash equivalents, and short- and long-term investments totaled $1.9 billion, and it has no debt. Divided by the roughly 430 million Class A and Class B shares outstanding on June 30, that's about $4.41 per share. That means cash and investments equal around 78% of Monday's closing price. And with no net income to measure the stock against, that cash is arguably the best gauge. NuScale's filing for its newest stock offering put its net tangible book value (assets minus liabilities, not counting intangibles like goodwill) even higher, at $4.63 per share at the end of June. So a buyer at $5.69 pays a bit over $1 per share (about $450 million in all) for everything else -- the reactor technology, the engineering team, and whatever orders eventually come through partner ENTRA1 Energy. NuScale has almost no revenue yet, just $75,000 for the second quarter of 2026, down from $8.1 million a year before. Still, the company doesn't burn cash very fast. Its operating activities used $314.7 million in the first quarter of 2026. But $259.9 million of that was one payment to ENTRA1. Take that payment out, and the company used around $55 million of cash over those three months, then about $58 million from April through June. That rate is accelerating, though, up from about $33 million in the second quarter of 2025. Losses are rising, too. NuScale's operating loss was $64 million in the second quarter -- 49% higher than a year before and over the first quarter's $58 million. That said, at roughly $230 million a year, $1.9 billion could fund several years of spending. Cash likely isn't NuScale's short-term issue.

But every leg down makes Oklo's next stock sale cost shareholders more, so I'd wait for customer money to carry more of the build before buying.

Nuclear energy stocks are becoming closely tied to the data center build-out. Alphabet's Google recently signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with Constellation Energy, the U.S.'s largest nuclear operator, to support its growing power needs. After its Oct. 6 announcement, Constellation's stock soared 12%, and other nuclear energy stocks followed suit. One intriguing stock in the space is NuScale Power (NYSE: SMR), an early-stage developer of small modular reactors (SMRs). As hyperscale data center operators search for dependable, carbon-free electricity, NuScale could offer investors another way to capitalize on the nuclear energy revival. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » The early-stage company trades below $6 per share and is largely story-driven, but one key catalyst could send the stock soaring. NuScale's Power Modules are factory-built SMRs that are based on light-water reactor technology. Each module produces 77 MWe (megawatt-electric) of power and can be deployed in multiunit arrays to provide up to 924 MWe, enough to power 700,000 homes or heavy-duty infrastructure such as data centers or industrial plants. The stock surged last year as data center investments ramped up and the Department of Energy took steps to boost the nuclear energy industry. As part of these efforts, the U.S. has an aggressive goal of quadrupling nuclear energy capacity by 2050 and is building traditional power plants while accelerating the development of microreactor and SMR technology. Over the past year, the stock has plunged. After peaking at around $57 per share, NuScale is down over 90%. Several factors are driving the decline, including weakness in nuclear energy stocks, Fluor (an early investor in NuScale) exiting its stake, and a lack of further commitments for its technology. NuScale has one project in Romania, but it needs more in its pipeline to gain real traction. One deal that could send the stock soaring is with the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA). NuScale is working with ENTRA1 to develop power plants, and on Sept. 2, 2025, ENTRA1 signed a non-binding agreement with the TVA for up to 6 gigawatts (GW) of power across its service region. The 6 GW project would be the largest SMR deployment in the U.S. and would require deploying up to 72 NuScale Power Modules. A deal would transform NuScale's long-term outlook.

Most Of NuScale Power's Market Value Is Cash Buyers of the stock acquire a large cash reserve first and a nuclear developer second. NuScale recorded a market value of about $2.64 billion at the October 15 close. At the end of June, the company held $1.89 billion in cash, short-term investments and longer-dated investments, and it carried no debt. That is about 72% of its market value. Subtracting those liquid assets reveals the price of the operating business itself, a metric investors refer to as enterprise value. For NuScale, that calculation lands at about $750 million. This represents the price paid for the reactor operations. That cash reserve remains in flux. Can NuScale Power Win Back Its Revenue? Executives maintain that revenue will rebound once a formal agreement is secured. That installation would deploy six NuScale power modules at a former coal plant site.

Over the past three years, NuScale Power's (NYSE: SMR) stock price has ranged from $2 to $53 per share. Today, it sits at a little under $8. Owning it has been a roller-coaster ride, with five drawdowns of 50% or more over that span. The current drawdown is the worst of them, at roughly 85%. That said, there's a clear event that could prompt investors to rethink their views of NuScale Power. The interesting thing about NuScale Power's huge price swings is that they aren't really driven by its business. That 85% decline didn't happen because of some terrible corporate disaster; it happened because investors got overly enthusiastic about nuclear power stocks, and then moved on to other things. NuScale Power, a nuclear power start-up at the leading edge of nuclear technology, simply went along for the ride. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » The technology NuScale Power is working on is small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs). It could be a game changer for the nuclear industry, as factory-built SMRs could be less costly, safer, and easier to place near where they are needed than current large-scale reactors. But the hard truth is that NuScale Power hasn't even built its first commercial SMR yet. It has an approved reactor design, which is a very big deal, but it still needs to find the first customer willing to sign on the dotted line. To the company's credit, it is working hard to ink that first sale. It has been working with the Romanian power company RoPower for quite some time and is seeing material success. RoPower has approved a project that would use six NuScale Power SMRs. But RoPower still needs to nail down project financing, so there's no agreement yet. NuScale Power is also working closely with ENTRA1 Energy and the Tennessee Valley Authority in hopes of being part of what could be "the largest nuclear power deployment program in U.S. history." But, like RoPower, there is still no deal yet. So, what the market is likely waiting for is NuScale Power's first SMR sale. That could be the event that pushes the stock back toward $20. However, it is important to remember that a signed contract is really just the start of the next stage of the company's development. Once it has that contract, it still needs to prove it can build an SMR and that the SMRs it builds are reliable and safe. In other words, NuScale Power is a high-risk start-up, and that isn't likely to change for quite some time.

NuScale Power (SMR) reported revenue of $0.1 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, compared with $8.1 million a year earlier. That number matters because NuScale is still spending to get its nuclear power modules ready to sell. The company recorded an operating loss of about $0.7 billion over the last twelve months, but most of it was a one-time payment of about $507 million to partner ENTRA1. In the latest quarter, the operating loss was about $64 million and operations used about $58 million of cash. So where did NuScale's revenue go? Why Did NuScale's Revenue Almost Disappear? Management attributed the revenue drop to the conclusion of a single piece of work. On an August 5, 2026 call, the company noted that Fluor engineering design work for the RoPower project in Romania finished in late 2025. Nothing comparable took its place in the latest quarter. The drop is not new, either. Revenue has fallen by more than 90% from a year earlier in each of the last three quarters, ending with a 99% contraction in the latest period. Over the last twelve months, revenue fell 81%. This compares with a 305% increase in the twelve months before that. NuScale's revenue appears to have depended on one specific project rather than a steady run of orders. NuScale Has About Two Years Of Cash NuScale ended June with about $1.9 billion in cash and investments, compared to a market value of about $2.5 billion today. Its debt sits at 0.0% of its market value, but its operations consumed about $0.8 billion in cash over the last twelve months. At that pace, the cash would last a little over two years. The stock fell 84% over the past twelve months, while the S&P 500 returned 17.3%. NuScale still sells for 228.5 times revenue, against 3.1 for the index. The current valuation likely assumes that a contract is coming. What Could Bring NuScale's Revenue Back? Management points to a signed customer contract as the solution. NuScale partner ENTRA1 is negotiating a definitive power purchase agreement with the Tennessee Valley Authority. Management stated its understanding is that those talks are active and progressing. It identified the commercial contract as the main catalyst but offered no timeline on the August 5 call. NuScale has some things in its favor while it waits. Management noted it remains the only company in its field holding design certification from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Furthermore, the company's forgings, the components that take the longest to manufacture, have been in production for two years. The RoPower project in Romania plans to deploy six NuScale power modules. NuScale stated on the August 5 call that it is waiting for a new government to approve the final contracts.

The NuScale Power Module™, the company's groundbreaking SMR technology, is a small, safe, pressurized water reactor that can each generate 77 megawatts of electricity (MWe) or 250 megawatts thermal (gross), and can be scaled to meet customer needs through an array of flexible configurations up to 924 MWe (12 modules) of output. There is growing hype for nuclear energy stocks. The thesis is simple: Providers of artificial intelligence (AI) are investing aggressively to build data centers. It's one of the biggest building booms in recent history. Data centers are energy-intensive, and because demand in many parts of the world has flatlined in recent years, current grid infrastructure isn't suited to handle a multiyear ramp-up in demand. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » With more generation capacity needed, nuclear looks like an ideal solution. According to research by Goldman Sachs: "Nuclear power will be a key part of a suite of new energy infrastructure built to meet surging data-center power demand driven by artificial intelligence. In the U.S. alone, big tech companies have signed new contracts for more than 10 GW of possible new nuclear capacity in the last year, and Goldman Sachs Research sees potential for three plants to be brought on line by 2030." Nuclear power is an ideal solution, given that it can deliver a huge amount of reliable, low-carbon electricity. But there's a problem: Nuclear power plants often cost billions of dollars to build, with construction sometimes stretching for a decade or more. AI companies need new power sources fast, and they want to avoid diverting capital away from building more computing infrastructure. Experts increasingly view small modular reactors, or SMRs, as solutions to this challenge. Bank of America says, "[N]ew advancements in technology may now make the tipping point in sight for small modular reactors to reshape nuclear energy supply chains over the next decade." The bank sees five major advantages for SMRs: lower up-front costs, improved safety, lower carbon emissions, smaller footprints, and the ability to modularize. Want to gain exposure to SMRs? Dozens of companies are pursuing the technology worldwide, but most are either privately held or part of a larger, more diversified conglomerate. Fortunately, three stocks with meaningful SMR exposure are currently publicly traded. Oklo (NYSE: OKLO) is betting that AI providers will want to control their means of energy production. The company intends to finance and construct their own plants near data center infrastructure, selling the energy production to AI companies through long-term power purchase agreements.

Energy Fuels Inc. UUUU and Cameco Corporation CCJ are well positioned to benefit from strengthening global demand for nuclear energy and the resulting need for reliable uranium supplies. While Energy Fuels is ramping up uranium production and expanding its rare earth elements (REE) business to capture opportunities across the critical materials value chain, Cameco leverages its large-scale uranium operations, diversified nuclear fuel cycle capabilities and strategic investments in nuclear technology to support long-term growth. For investors seeking exposure to the nuclear energy sector, the two companies offer distinct investment propositions. Comparing their operating performance, growth prospects, earnings estimates and valuations can help determine which stock offers the more attractive risk-reward profile today. Energy Fuels has produced nearly two-thirds of all uranium in the United States since 2017. The company is scaling up uranium production while investing in rare earth processing and downstream capabilities to capitalize on growing demand for nuclear fuel and critical materials. In the second quarter of 2026, Energy Fuels mined approximately 315,000 pounds of uranium, bringing first-half production to 740,000 pounds. Finished uranium production reached 865,000 pounds in the quarter and 1.7 million pounds in the first half, exceeding the low end of its full-year production guidance of 1.5-2.5 million pounds. The company expects to mine 2-2.5 million pounds of contained uranium in 2026 and sell 1.5-2 million pounds through spot and contracted transactions. In March 2026, it successfully produced terbium (Tb) oxide at pilot scale, becoming the first U.S. company in decades to achieve this milestone. In August, its terbium oxide was qualified by one of the world's largest rare earth permanent magnet manufacturers outside China, marking progress toward commercializing its heavy rare earth capabilities. Energy Fuels' second-quarter revenues jumped 496% year over year to $25.1 million, driven by higher uranium sales volumes and realized prices. The company sold 310,000 pounds of uranium at an average realized price of $80.48 per pound compared with 50,000 pounds at $77 per pound in the year-ago quarter. Costs applicable to revenues surged 192% to $10.7 million on higher uranium volumes sold, partially offset by lower weighted average cost per pound of uranium sold. Standby costs surged 61% year over year due to higher permitting activities at Roca Honda and Whirlwind and increased maintenance activities at Nichols Ranch. Selling, general and administration were up 31% year over year, reflecting increases in general headcount, salaries and benefits. UUUU also incurred $10.7 million in transaction and integration costs. The company reported a net loss of 13 cents per share in the quarter, wider than the year-ago quarter's loss of 10 cents per share. The company has six uranium supply contracts with U.S. nuclear utilities with deliveries extending to 2032. As of June 30, 2026, contracted volumes totaled 3.20 million base pounds, with minimum and maximum deliveries of 2.77 million and 4.72 million pounds, respectively. Energy Fuels has a substantial pipeline of uranium development projects. The Whirlwind mine and Nichols Ranch ISR project alone could add up to 500,000 pounds of annual uranium production within a year of a development decision. Other major projects, including Roca Honda, Bullfrog and Sheep Mountain, collectively contain nearly 70 million pounds of uranium resources.

To put a number on that, in the U.S. market, electricity demand increased by 10% between 2005 and 2025, but is projected to grow by 60% between 2025 and 2045. That's a step change in demand, driven by power-hungry technologies like artificial intelligence and electric vehicles, among other things. Nuclear power is likely to be a big beneficiary, given that it doesn't produce greenhouse gases and is always available, unlike solar and wind. There are currently 417 operating reactors worldwide, with another 77 under construction. Cameco estimates the demand for uranium will outstrip supply in the early 2030s. That's important because Cameco mines uranium and produces nuclear fuel. More reactors mean more customers for Cameco to sell to. And since uranium is a commodity, demand outstripping supply will likely mean higher commodity prices. So Cameco's uranium operation is a picks-and-shovels play on nuclear power. But Cameco also own half of Westinghouse, one of the world's largest service providers to the nuclear power industry. That business provides more reliable cash flows, helping to balance the more volatile uranium operation. And, once again, more reactors means more customers. Unless the world decides en masse to abandon nuclear power, Cameco looks well-positioned to benefit from the nuclear comeback.

The stock then rebounded from $85 in late July to $107 in August and gave the whole gain back, even after Jefferies and TD Cowen initiated at buy with C$190 targets on September 3. Cameco Acknowledges United States and Republic of Korea Announcement of Framework for the Deployment of Nuclear Power

No summary available

All amounts in Canadian dollars unless specified otherwise This news release constitutes a "designated news release" for the purposes of Cameco's prospectus supplement dated November 12, 2024, to its short form base shelf prospectus dated November 12, 2024. SASKATOON, Saskatchewan, September 30, 2...

All amounts in Canadian dollars unless specified otherwise This news release constitutes a "designated news release" for the purposes of Cameco's prospectus supplement dated November 12, 2024, to its short form base shelf prospectus dated November 12, 2024. SASKATOON, Saskatchewan, September 30, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Cameco Corporation (TSX: CCO; NYSE: CCJ) acknowledges that the United States of America ("USG") and the Republic of Korea ("Korea"), under a previously entered Memorandum of Understanding (the "MOU"), today announced a framework that anticipates the investment by Korea of US$120 billion to help finance the buildout of Westinghouse reactor technology in the US using expertise and companies from both nations (the "Framework"). The Framework, which is separate and unrelated to the Department of Energy's American Nuclear Supply Chain Loans conditional commitment, contemplates the construction of up to eight large nuclear reactors in the United States, including six Westinghouse AP1000® reactors and up to two Korean APR1400 reactors that are built on Westinghouse technology. If successfully concluded, both technologies are expected to be deployed on federal sites designated by the USG, beginning with the deployment of two AP1000 reactors, contributing to the expansion of clean, reliable and domestically produced nuclear energy generation capacity. Building upon the strategic partnership announcement between Cameco, Brookfield Asset Management and the United States Department of Commerce in October 2025 (the "Partnership"), this Framework outlines a potential funding and execution pathway for the construction of new nuclear reactors in the United States under the Partnership. The Framework is subject to the negotiation and execution of definitive agreements, identification of planning of specific sites, regulatory approvals, financing arrangements, other customary conditions, and the finalization of definitive agreements under the Partnership. The Framework contemplates a waiver under the 2025 settlement agreement reached by Westinghouse in its intellectual property dispute with Korea Electric Power Corporation and Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power Co., Ltd. The one-time waiver would allow for the construction of up to two APR1400 reactors in the United States, generating enhanced value for Westinghouse. The associated compensation package is expected to recognize the use of Westinghouse intellectual property and technology, providing approximately US$2 billion of value per APR1400 reactor through a combination of intellectual property licensing, engineering and procurement services, subcontracting opportunities and the long-term supply of fuel fabrication services, highlighting the strategic role that Westinghouse is expected to play across the contemplated reactor projects in the US.

Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) has been a polarizing stock since its record-breaking IPO in June. Some investors are deeply impressed by the company's innovations and expect it to deliver life-changing returns over the long run, while others are skeptical, especially given valuation concerns. Which side is right? Perhaps it's still too early to decide, but it is at least fair to say that SpaceX gave the bulls more robust arguments with its latest quarterly update. Let's look into it. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Image source: The Motley Fool. The market had fairly high expectations for SpaceX's third-quarter results. The company met these expectations, and then some. SpaceX's revenue soared by 161% year over year to $14.6 billion. While SpaceX is perhaps best known for its space launch services, the company's two other segments, connectivity and Super Intelligence (SI), performed significantly better. Space revenue increased just 6% year over year to $1.8 billion. Connectivity sales jumped 69.5% year over year to $5.2 billion, and SI revenue was $7.6 billion, up 830% compared to the year-ago period. True, SpaceX's SI unit benefited from an acquisition that closed in August, adding $608 million in revenue to the segment. But even without that, SI sales would have grown 755% year over year. SpaceX's connectivity and SI businesses were both profitable during the quarter, with the former posting an operating income of $2.4 billion, up 99% year over year. SI's operating income of $431 million came in well above the operating loss of $1.7 billion reported in the same period of the previous fiscal year. On the bottom line, the company posted a net income of $4.4 billion, significantly better than the prior-year quarter's net loss of $1.1 billion. SpaceX's CEO, Elon Musk, has said the company could generate $1 trillion in revenue by 2030, and perhaps even by 2029. Recent financial results certainly make this goal more achievable, but it's still an ambitious target. Can SpaceX pull it off? On the one hand, the company's SI and connectivity businesses are firing on all cylinders and could tap into highly lucrative opportunities over the medium term. Third-quarter SI sales grew rapidly partly because the company added several artificial intelligence (AI) cloud services agreements. There is clearly significant demand for AI compute capacity, and SpaceX is cashing in on that.

Price targets are supposed to tell you where a stock is headed. Sometimes they mostly tell you how much an analyst is willing to believe. When I wrote about SpaceX's IPO buyers in September, the stock had already split them into very different outcomes depending on when they got in. Every new forecast since has pulled that crowd in a different direction. The company handed the bulls plenty of fuel this week. SpaceX's revenue jumped 161% to $14.6 billion in the third quarter, and it swung to a $4.4 billion profit from a $1.1 billion loss, according to Quartz. Elon Musk said on the Oct. 20 call that he is "fairly confident" SpaceX can add about 10 gigawatts of computing capacity in 2027. That is the kind of number that makes Wall Street rewrite its spreadsheets overnight. JPMorgan analyst Doug Anmuth raised his SpaceX price target to $500 from $240 on Oct. 21 and kept an Overweight rating, Investing.com reported. The new target implies 238% upside from the stock's $147.79 close on Oct. 20. Anmuth more than doubled his 2027 and 2028 estimates. JPMorgan now models 10 gigawatts of compute by the end of 2027 and total 2027 revenue of $254 billion, the report said. That points to an annual revenue run rate of about $400 billion by the end of 2027. Management's own range is far higher, at $500 billion to $1 trillion, Investing.com reported. Related: Vivian Tu's IPO warning lands as SpaceX buyers split by $1,851 Most of that growth has to come from artificial intelligence. SpaceX's Super Intelligence segment brought in $7.6 billion in the third quarter, up 830%, while its connectivity business grew 69% to $5.2 billion, Quartz reported. The target rests on 20 times JPMorgan's 2028 earnings estimate of $24.41 a share. I ran that math, and it works out to about $488, so the published $500 either rounds up or uses a slightly richer multiple than the summary describes. Shares had already moved before the note landed. The stock rose 6.6% after hours to $157.59 on Oct. 20, according to Investing.com, as revenue beat the $12.87 billion that analysts expected. JPMorgan is far out ahead of its peers, and the size of that gap is the real story in this week's notes. Here is where other banks landed after the report, according to Investing.com: Morgan Stanley: Kept an Overweight rating and a $300 target while raising its AI revenue forecasts, Investing.com reported. UBS: Raised its target to $230, citing strength in AI compute leasing, the same report showed. RBC Capital: Reiterated Outperform with a $225 target, pointing to a favorable long-term outlook. Mizuho: Raised its target to $205 with an Outperform rating after revenue and adjusted EBITDA beat its own forecasts. Stifel: Reiterated a Buy rating and a $190 target.
